We ourselves got into a bad situation.

s: Nonbíx íti riki náshii; moa noa ján ímaira yámake.
e: We are going to bathe by ourselves, because the one who supervises us at the bath is not here.

s: Máto pátoron betan téeyamai, matónbinix téetakayara íti iki jakónyora.
e: It would be much better if you just worked among yourselves.

s: Rámara aínbobo jatónbinix pirótanin tsíniai; moátianra bénbobaon ímakatitai.
e: Nowadays women play soccer by themselves; formerly, the men guided them.
The Campa fought among themselves.

Some boys burned this house.
Pepe and his companions burned this house.
white-lipped peccaries together with others (e.g., collared peccaries and pigs) of the same genus

s: Topónwe chónkabo chónkabo asta pácha kaman.
e: Count by tens up to a hundred.

s: Non boánhis jene xéaara ísiman ítima iki.
e: When we drink the juice of the sacha ajo, illnesses rarely attack us.

s: Nato neténra ícha jóni boánke Máioshiain boí.
e: Today many people passed by on their way to Pucallpa.

s: Jawen bobónki pirótanin tsákaara nato jonín máxkaxon mái tsákake.
e: This man fell to the ground unconscious when the ball struck his infected sore.
The ants stung my little boy and gave him little boils.

s: Nokon maponkora ea bobónke, binán tékaa.
e: Boils broke out on my head because the wasp stung me.

s: Pítsokori piáx bonbónketianra rókotoron báke raónke.
e: The doctor treated the child who had boils from having eaten matamata.

s: Abion bóchiki wínotainbira non mérayamake, ishtóira iken.
e: Even though the airplane was passing overhead, we could not locate it because it was going very fast.

s: Xóbo bochiki báwa nóyainbira kampán tsákake, mécha ixon.
e: Even though the parrot was flying high above the house, the Campa shot it with an arrow, for he was a good hunter.

s: Nato tasára moa naránxa bócho iki.
e: This basket is already full of oranges.
I filled the canoe with many palm leaves.
The masato (a fermented drink) filled up in Mother's jar.
Upriver there is a mijanada (a fish migration) of boquichicos.

s: En koshóshka cháchiara ea bóeati boónke.
e: I speared a river dolphin without realizing it, and it carried off my huahuasapa.
The combs the trader has brought are very expensive.

s: Xena píi íitaitianra en boín tsákake.
e: While the woodpecker was eating grubs, I shot it with an arrow.

s: Bójaro riki tóro jisá, ikaxbi ánichabires.
e: The buffalo resembles the bull, but is a bit larger.
One-armed people eat papaya.

s: En bokékin jankénhaamabira titán kawín bóke.
e: Although I had not finished interweaving the reeds of the mat at the ends, mother took it away.
When the gunboat came, our ancestors were afraid.
The dog took the roasted intestines of the taricaya (a river turtle) out of the fire and carried them off.

s: Nato simánaninra nokon bokón tapan en Máioshiain bóai.
e: This week I will take my cetico-wood raft to Pucallpa.

s: Moátianronki ból jóniakana shinón tímanike joni shinankin.
e: They say that in ancient times the monkey punched a human-shaped figure of tar, thinking it was a person.
The sorcerer has come to curse the thief.

s: Oa chipónkiax joá jónira bománya iki.
e: That man who has come from downriver is a cursing sorcerer.

s: Kóka Ikítoain káitianra titán jawen téoti bómake.
e: When my uncle was about to go to Iquitos, my mother sent his necklaces with him so he would sell them.

s: Moa kírika bomá ikáxbira, ishtón jóni jóyamaiki.
e: Although a letter had been sent to him, the man did not come right away.

s: Néno ika mibé ráenanaibaonra, mia sároro bómakanai.
e: Your good friends who are here send you greetings.
A hat made from the shoot of the bombonaje palm is very expensive.
Nowadays they make necklaces out of the heads of the *bómpa* beetle.

s: Bakísh píshta íkaitianra yame bómpo íishinai.
e: They are going to play the bass drum all night, because tomorrow is a fiesta.
A certain little old man died from an isula sting.

s: Níi meran bóna bénaitianra jóni oín mecháake.
e: While the man was looking for bees in the monte (forest), the rain soaked him.

s: Non bónajene íchayora xéaaronki chikíshti iki.
e: They say that if we drink too much bee honey, we can grow weak.
The *bonánchai* ant does not sting us.
The child fell off the top of the trunk.
A man had his case stolen.
This gluttonous man is stingy.
In ancient times the Bonchibo were very fierce.

s: Bóexeetama ikax bonchón íketianra, jawen maístoron nato báke kastíkanke.
e: The teacher punished this boy for having his hair bristly and uncombed.

s: Papánra manánxawe bíke káchio kaxón bonkánaman rákata.
e: While going through the monte (forest), father caught a motelo (tortoise) that was lying under a *bonká* palm.

s: Jóni jenén rétea íketianra en bonkéake joimakaskin.
e: I moved the drowned man's head from side to side to make him breathe.
This child moves his head from side to side to show that he does not want to cultivate.

s: Jawen pátoronin téeti bókasara kakáshamai bonkéke.
e: When his boss wanted to take him to work, he shook his head from side to side because he did not want to go.
With hard work I made a garden plot in the virgin forest.

s: Xóbibo óroxonra en jaínbicho tsamánxon bónkoake.
e: When I cleared the weeds, I piled them up in one place, forming a thicket.
Since I bought many aluminum pots, I piled them up.

s: Nokon wáira moa jákiribi bónkoa iki, en óroyamaa.
e: My garden plot has turned back into forest because I have not cultivated it.
The fruit of the aguaje (moriche palm) forms up high, in clusters of many fruits.

s: Káchiora isán bimi bónkoa en mérake.
e: In the monte (forest) I saw some ungurahui (palm) fruits piled up.
They say that the demon of the copaiba tree is a very tall man.

s: Bonsín riki ochíti keska, ikáxbi yobé.
e: The otter is very much like a dog, but it is a bewitched animal.
A mouse ate the little *bóntoish* bird that mother was raising.

s: Non bónxaman shinánronki béroyoshiman náikan bóai.
e: They say that when we die, the spirit of the pupil of the eye carries our thoughts, which reside in our lungs, up to the sky.
He grabbed me by the hair, but I made him let go.

s: Nato aínbora jawen rérakaata bóo ikáinbi ronón natéxke.
e: The snake bit this woman on the spot where a cut she had had healed.
They say that with chuchuhuasi (a medicinal plant) cuts heal quickly.

s: Ráma nétera non boró tsékakanai, bakísha non óroibake.
e: Today we are pulling up the rootstocks that we planted yesterday.
When he was crossing the stream on foot, an aquatic *borón* jergón bit him.
They stole my bag in Pucallpa.

s: Sísion ákaibora en winókin óina bóroxa iki.
e: As I passed by there, I saw that only the heads of those who were in the meeting were showing.
Yesterday my uncle brought a baby chosna from the monte (forest).
They say that the puñuisiqui fish emerged from a man's penis.
This Brazilian has kinky hair.
A mestizo woman curled my daughter's hair.
This woman curled her hair in Lima.

s: Titán póa joara moa wáaketian bóteke.
e: Mom took the boiled sachapapa (an edible tuber) off the fire because it was already done.
The pig shoved the metal pot that had been taken off the fire.

s: Kókara jawen pátoronin téeti bóke Tamáyanin.
e: My uncle was taken by his boss to work on the Tamaya river.
There are many medicines in the pharmacy.
We store salt in bottles.

s: Non botón píketianronki non báke chíxotai.
e: They say that if we eat concompes, our children may get diarrhea.
When the boy swallowed the button, the doctor took it out.

s: Non bóya méeketianronki báke kópia bépoai.
e: They say that if we touch a *bóya* hive, our children become cutipados (afflicted by supernatural harm) and begin to secrete a lot of eye discharge.
Getting stuck in the mud, the child could not get out despite his efforts.

s: Papán jawen nónti bóyaara moa jéne béyamai.
e: Since dad caulked his canoe, no water gets in.

s: Moa bóyakana ikénbira papán nonti bóyakanke.
e: Dad's canoe had been patched, but they took it away.

s: Nokon xéta péketaton ea chéxayoraitianra, en rókotoro bóyamake.
e: The dentist filled my decayed tooth that hurt me so much.

s: Nato bonánti tíayamakanwe; moa boyá ríki.
e: Don't touch this trunk, because it has been patched.
without the use of both legs
Going a little farther, he arrived.

s: ¿Jáweratoki nénkecha iki, papán nónti o epána?
e: Which is longer, papa's canoe or uncle's?
They say that when the little *cháa* bird sings at night, it is a sign of bad omen.
The father opened the door with the key.
Mama painted papa's face with little dots of achiote (a red dye plant).

s: Jawen chachí isín íketianra pápa jóyamai.
e: Papa cannot come because his sting hurts him.

s: Rámara mia rabé chachíres maxkáke —akinra ea rókotoron áke.
e: The doctor told me that now I only have two injections left.
The bagre (a catfish) is a fish that pricks because it has spines.

s: Atapa benekira ea ráketai, ea chachinaketian.
e: I am afraid the rooster is going to peck me.
When I speared the caiman, it carried off my harpoon.
The health worker gave him an injection because the fever would not leave him.

s: Moa kopíora ikénbira ea cháchitinin mároke.
e: I bought a syringe even though it was very expensive.

s: Nokon bákera cháchitiki ráketai, moa íchaakin ákana ikax.
e: My son is afraid of injections, because they have been given to him many times.
Playing with the needle, she pricked herself on the hand.
They gave me an injection at the clinic.
ea pikóke. While playing soccer, I felt a stabbing pain and left the game.
His brother-in-law does not pay him, even though he owes him.

s: Noa cháikonin yótoaronki jími kínani noa máwatai.
e: They say that when the forest spirit *cháikoni* bewitches us, we can die from vomiting blood.

s: Jíwi chaíshakin ráteara nato báke winike.
e: This child got scared and cried when a dry branch of the tree broke.
The branch broke and made a sudden sound.
This child wants to eat mashed plantain.
When the plantain swells, it splits.

s: Mái chaká ikain jámataxa jóni taskéke.
e: When stepping on the cracked ground, the man dislocated his foot.

s: Bákera meskéke mái chaká meran káax.
e: The child broke his hand when he fell into the crevice in the ground.
When the waves beat against our boat, we capsized.

s: Nóntiki bechón chakásh ikinra báke jéne xéamake.
e: When the waves beat against the canoe, water got into the child's mouth.
The carpenter smashed his hand.
My grandfather makes a harpoon by hammering a piece of iron.
My papa smashed his finger with a hammer.

s: Non paránta chákataronki aínbo bakeati iki.
e: They say that when the plantain splits for some reason, it means we will have a daughter.
In the dry season, the ground cracks.
They say that when it is about to rain, the little *cháki* toad sings.
Come here, little boy.
You eat like pigs, chewing noisily.

s: Jaínra xánbo kai chamá —íkira ikánke bákebo já bénai.
e: Looking for lagarscissors, the children would say —There goes one, friend!

s: Néri jowé chamá noa wéxaananon —ikira jóni íkai.
e: The man says to his enemy —Come fight, scoundrel.
They say the smallpox demon looks like a white man.

s: En poróto bánaabira ea champón kéyonaanke.
e: The crickets destroyed the beans I planted.
They say the wasp's compadre is the little paucar.
My dad did not go to drink, even though they had invited him.

s: Nonra xéatiapariai; jákopira chánitain noa káyamai.
e: We are going to keep preparing the drink, and that is why we are not yet going to where we are invited.

s: Moátianronki iká iki westíora mápijoni, jawen béro chánka.
e: They tell that in ancient times there was a shrimp-man who had protruding eyes.
Stand it up there.
Although he did not know how to walk, this child stood up

s: Nato aínbora bóexeetama iki; jawen bóora chánkata iki.
e: This woman is not combed; her hair is standing up

s: Noa chánkati kakénbira noa kénakana jóke.
e: We had gone visiting but came back, because our family called us.
This child walks on tiptoe because he stepped on a thorn.
The protuberances on his body have disappeared thanks to the injection he was given.
They say that when a hen eats fariña (manioc meal), the cuchipe attacks it.
My granny died when protuberances appeared on her body.
My hens have caught cuchipe.
They say that if we laugh at the matamata, boils resembling its protuberances may break out on us.

s: Nato bísikirita chántara en otsíaama iki; nato jonínra áke.
e: I did not deflate the tire of this bicycle; this man did it.

s: Jatíbi jawen yóra jakón ikáxbira chántores iki.
e: He is in good health, in spite of being lame.

s: Nato bákera jawen titán chántoake sináxon.
e: That boy was made lame by his mother in a moment of anger.

s: Jonínra jawen báke chántoake sontáro kámakaxamakin.
e: A man made his son limp so that he would not go into the army.
They say the water of the *chantómari* spring is not potable.

s: Kimisha óxe ísinaxa nokon báke chántoke.
e: My little son became lame because he was ill for three months.

s: Nokon táera en chapáake rérakin, jíwi ati shinánkin.
e: When I meant to cut the tree, I accidentally cut my foot.

s: Nokon mekén chapatainkora ea bonán tékake.
e: A isula (bullet ant) stung me in a crease between my fingers.
Dad shot the coto (howler monkey) that was sitting in the fork.
The motor (motorboat) capsized upstream at the confluence of this river.
The Ucayali River forks at its end (that is, at the confluence of the Tambo and Urubamba rivers).

s: Nato bái káara moa sénenain chapáke.
e: The road ahead forks at the end.

s: Jawen titán asókaro charáakatoninra nato báke menóke.
e: This child got burned by the sugar his mother had melted.
I am melting copal (a tree resin) to caulk the canoe.

s: En ípo bachi biábira barín charáake.
e: The carachama (armored catfish) eggs I got melted in the sun.
The group of tied cañabravas (wild cane) that I threw down rattled as they fell to the ground

s: Epán charánwa beá pikáshamaira báke wíniai.
e: The child cries because he does not want to eat the achacubo his uncle has brought.
Dad is shaking his arrows.

s: Barín akára nokon téri charáke, en bénxoayamaa.
e: I did not put away the *téri* pitch, and it melted from the heat of the sun.

s: Titán átsa jóaara jéne kéyotax yámikenti charáke.
e: The water of the manioc mom was cooking dried up and the aluminum pot melted down.
The katalán's chick is very plump.
They tell that once a katalán-man married a woman.
The shamiros devour the corn dad planted.

s: Moátianronki westíora yósishokoki matsín charíshaa nókokanike.
e: They tell that in ancient times they came by chance upon a little old man stiffened by the cold.

s: Aínbo máwatara moa charíshke, rabé néte ikax.
e: The dead woman's body stiffened because two days had passed since she died.

s: Moa kabórinin cháro jokonaitianronki jóo kéotai.
e: They say that when the taricaya (a river turtle) hatchlings come out of the eggs, the gualos (a kind of toad) sing.

s: Wáiroronra jato yatánxon charónke jato katónoxon.
e: The guard recruited them and lined them up to select them for the army.
The thief stepped on the upright nails dad had set.

s: Jatíbi jónira kampón charóke tsínikanai óini.
e: All the people are standing in the field watching the players.

s: Noa bénotaxbira noa jóke chashí méraaxes.
e: We had gotten lost in the monte (the forest), but came back only because we found the little broken branches marking the trail.
I had no machete; I just broke off a few little branches.
Without my touching it, it broke.
They say that when someone is lazy, he should drink the juice of the *cháwa* vine.
The drunk man wallowed in the mud.
The path became muddy from the rain.

s: Nokon chaín wíntianoxon jíwi cháxaara jóni yómetsoke.
e: A man stole the timber my brother-in-law had hewn to make a paddle.
They tell that the motelos (tortoises) killed a deer by wearing it out.
The dog carried off the deer-hide strap mom had tied on.
They say that back when people worked the rubber trade, they used to eat *chaxóx* tadpoles.

s: Icha néte náshimayamakinra aínbaon jawen báke cheáake.
e: A mother made her child anemic by not bathing him for many days.
He became posheco from the habit of eating clay.
The hawk carried off the *cheí* parakeet that mom had raised.
He cried because his brother tickled him.
This child smells of urine.

s: Nokon kotónra ochítinin chékoake, jáki jisónxon.
e: A dog made my shirt smell of urine because it urinated on it.

s: Chómomea ompáxa moa chékoa iki, moa rabé simána ikax.
e: The water in the jug has a stale smell because it has been there for two weeks already.

s: Jénetianra cheó kéotai jawen báchi potai.
e: During the flood season the chiuchiu frogs call out when they release their eggs.

s: Jawen títa máxokan réteketianra átapa bakeshokobo cheónkicheonkiikai.
e: The chicks cheep because the fox killed their mother.
They say that when horseflies are burned, they multiply.
While the cattle slept in the middle of the pasture, the horsefly fed by biting them.

s: Titán jonokishi xóia xéni chéretaira papán átsapotoya méskoxon píke.
e: Dad mixed the fat rendered from the sajino (collared peccary) leg mom roasted with fariña and ate it.

s: Wáme nami xóia chéretaira ochítinin táxoke.
e: The dog licked up the fat that rendered from the roasted paiche meat.
There was medicine for the pain.

s: Ea shetán chéxaketianra, en rókotoro tsékamake.
e: The dentist pulled my tooth when it hurt.
Today at dawn she began to have labor pains.
Even though I painted my face with huito, it is not very black.
Mom blackened the water by putting huito in it.

s: Nanén síkitara nato aínbaon bémanan chéxea iki.
e: This woman's face turned black because she painted it with huito.
to tie by the buttocks
small worms in the anus
to sniff at the rear parts
to back up
tailless
half a cañabrava (cane) placed crosswise on the eaves
to sit in the stern

with a strong base
a species of four-pointed arrow
to cut at the handle
When I hung the mosquito net, the mosquitoes got in.

s: Westíora chíaraxti kopira jawen pátoronin rabé konxán xate bichínke.
e: For the price of a pair of trousers his boss charged him two logs of cedar.
Young people today do not want to learn to make the *chíati* knife.
The boy took my mother's beater (weaving stick).
There is no one in the mosquito net that is hung taut.

s: Nokon waránka sóro boónketianra en chibánxon bichínke.
e: When he stole my thousand soles, I followed him and took it back.

s: Moa néno bási ixónbira nato lamístonin chibíti onányamake.
e: This person from Lamas does not know how to steer even though he has been here a long time.
They say the smell of a goat cutipa (causes sympathetic illness) in a baby.
They are singing under the large eaves of the house.
The boil I have on my buttock hurts.

s: Non chichínra noa jatíbi áti yóiai.
e: Our maternal grandmother gives the orders.

s: Nato yantán sísion átira jatón chichín jato kénai.
e: The supreme authority calls them to a session tonight.
The boys threw away grandfather's knife.
A mijanada (mass migration) of shiripira fish is going down the river.
The *chichíporo* bird has the habit of nesting in houses.

s: Bémakayanra jakónira iki nato chómo; jawen chichóra jakóma iki.
e: This jar looks very pretty on the outside, but its interior is ugly.

s: Pishtákobaon rétenaketianra nokon pápa xóbo chichó jonéke.
e: My father hid deep inside the house so the pishtacos would not kill him.

s: Jéne chichó káketianra westíora aínbo jenén réteke.
e: A woman drowned from going too deep into the water.
My trunk is inside.
So the thieves would not find it, I put the money deep inside.

s: En piróta jámata káaxa chíiki pakéke.
e: The ball I kicked rolled and fell into the fire.
Toads swallow firebrands.
They say that demons of that kind have eyes like firebrands.
They tell that a woman in a coma saw hell.

s: Chíi yámaketianra non chíimakaman káro ketéake.
e: For lack of fire, we lit the firewood with the spark of a stone.
At carnival they even painted themselves with ashes.

s: Jawen épán chikároninra papán wáme cháchike.
e: Dad speared the paiche with his uncle's harpoon.
The pig got out by breaking the fence.
Our school has wooden walls.
**kaxón píti iki.** They say that when we go visiting and see a little *chíki* hawk on the path, we are sure to be given food.

s: En chíkiraya mashín bánaara ea kokámebaon keyónke.
e: The cowpeas that I planted on the beach were all harvested by some cocamas.

s: Westíora jonínra jawen báke chikísh ímake, jatíbitian téetiain íoyamakin.
e: A certain man got his son used to being lazy by never taking him to work.

s: Ichayora mishkín kókoaxa nato jóni chikíshke.
e: This man became lazy from eating a great deal of honey.
They say that the call of the *chikóro* demon announces the arrival of visitors.
My paternal uncle's house has no *chikóshkinti* crossbeams.
-aquin aká iqui. He told her: -If you spill it, I won't give you any more.
The pig licks up the spilled drink.
When the jug broke, the water spilled.

s: Orobampa chimakayanra samán onsá iki; jaínra jóni réoke.
e: At the mouth of the Urubamba there is a very dangerous whirlpool that capsized a man in his canoe.

s: Nato táe chimakayainra en nónti pótake.
e: At the mouth of this caño I left the canoe.

s: En íwi cháchiara ea chimápo boónke.
e: When I speared a stingray, it carried off my *chimápo* arrow.

s: Nato chímiman póira náshiaitian jenén réteke.
e: This girl's little brother drowned while he was bathing.

s: Ráma yaméra chímpa xobo naman ránsakanai.
e: Tonight they are going to dance in a house made of crisnejas.

s: Ja chímpansi riki Ajírikamea íso, nekea isón ewa keskaribi. Ikaxbira jínaoma iki.
e: The chimpanzee is a monkey from Africa, similar to the large monkeys here, but without a tail.
A boy broke my sister's beaded belt.

s: Yamé íshtoira ea chiní meran káke.
e: Running at night, I fell into the excavation.

s: Koríke míinkana bíkanara mái chiní áni iki.
e: The excavation in the ground is large, the one where they found the hidden money.

s: Mia chiníora jóketianra mia namán kopíake.
e: Because you came last, they paid you less.

s: Eapari nokókasira ea chiníke motóro masáketian.
e: I hoped to arrive before the others, but I arrived last because the motor (outboard motor) broke down.
All these children were given an enema.
When my son's stomach swelled up, the doctor gave him an enema.
This child is afraid of the enema syringe.
My father killed a hummingbird with his bird-hunting arrow.
Don't bother your little brother's loro (parrot).

s: Bákeoma ixon jawen chiobakebi onánhan riki.
e: She adopted her own niece because she had no children.

s: Xóbo chipán namanra pápa páenax rakáke.
e: Papá is drunk and is lying down under the eaves of the house.
Mamá's new jar has a hole in the lower part.

s: Jawen chipéxko tóbitaxa nato báke chántoti níai.
e: This child limps because he dislocated his iliac bone.

s: Jaínra min chípi jóai káro papía.
e: There comes your older sister carrying firewood.

s: Moa chipónki káinbira jawen papán ráanyamake.
e: Even though he was already going downriver, his father did not send him.

s: Chiárextioma ikaxa nato báke kótoman chipóke.
e: This child covered himself with his shirt because he had no trousers.

s: Mia éki chipóketianra mia tsón jáweatima iki.

What animal ate this?

s: ¿Jawénki nato wísoino min rétea? —akinki jonín jawen awín aká iki.
e: They say a man asked his wife: 'What did you kill this yanapuma (black jaguar) with?'
qui mia Kakónkoniax joá? What did you come from Caco in?

s: Aínbaonronki jawen benén yamín íno rétenike.
e: They say that once a woman killed a jaguar (tigre) with her husband's axe.
Where is your father?
Where has my mother gone?
Where have you put the machete?
Where did you see my paternal uncle?
Where did you get the axe?
Where have you come from?
Where have you come from?

s: ¿Jáweranoxon akárin en mia jáskara jói yóikin?
e: At what place did I say such words to you about this matter?
In what direction did you want to go a while ago?

s: Jáweraoki mia kái, jáinra ea kái.
e: 'Which way are you going?' —'I'm going that way.'
What direction does this path we're taking go?
From approximately what place did the man shout?

s: Nenónxonbi mánawe, jaweraokeaxki jóai min oínon.
e: Wait right here to see from what direction he is coming.
From what direction did we hear them firing their weapons?
Which one do you want?
When are you going upriver?
At what times does the jaguar (tigre) move about?

s: Min nokon jói sénenhayamaitianra, en mia jáwetianbi kopíayamanox iki.
e: If you don't follow my orders, I will never pay you.
How many people have gone to Pucallpa?
What price is the pampanilla (traditional skirt) that you embroidered?
How big is the cut on his leg?

s: ¿Jáwetio naxbárin ja min papán bená nóntiaa?
e: How wide is the inside of the new canoe your father made?
How wide a stretch did you swim across the cocha (oxbow lake)?

s: ¿Jain áblon jéne meran káaki jáwetio nemín iki?
e: How deep is the place where the plane fell into the water?
Uncle, how long did you cut the wood?
From here, how far away is your town?

s: ¿Jáwetio keyá áni wapóroki min óina iki?
e: At what height did you see the big steamship?

s: ¿Papán ronón ewa méraaki jáwetio rastón iká?
e: The boa constrictor father saw — how thick was it?

s: Rámara paránta jaxká kikínbires kopí iki, mírikaronko.
e: Nowadays a hand of plantains is very expensive in the market.

s: Moátianronki jóniki inón jáxkayonike konxán xátei káketian.
e: They say that long ago, a man who had gone to cut cedar (cedro) was completely dismembered by a jaguar (tigre).
Falling from the top of a tree, the man tore off his arm.

s: En paránta texkan pápixon beára moa kéyoti jaxkáke.
e: The bunch of plantains I was carrying on my back has completely fallen apart.

s: Nokon épara píti bénai káshbi jayáoma jóke, jawen pía jéne meran káketian.
e: My paternal uncle went to hunt for game (mitayo); but he came back with nothing because his arrow fell into the water.

s: Amaabira, je, min ámaabira, je, warón rakáyamai, je. Era rakáyamai, je.
e: Although I take to drinking, although because of you I take to drinking, drunk I do not lie down. I do not lie down.

s: Moátianronki jéekanki áwakan poínki meran kaxón jawen joínti xaténike.
e: They say that long ago the pucacuru worm entered through the tapir's anus and killed it by cutting its heart.
Many people will settle in this cleared place.
In Caco, small planes land right in the middle of the street.

s: Nato nétera ápo nókotai non jéma óini.
e: Today a high-ranking official will arrive to visit our community.
They say that Paococha alone is the large Shipibo village.

s: Máioshinya jemánra moa yómetso ícha iki.
e: In the town of Pucallpa there are quite a lot of thieves these days.

s: Ichaxonra nato báritia réboki bená jémaakanke.
e: This year, many founded new settlements (colonias) upriver.
**jémaati shinánkanai.** The people of Cunchuri, who are not Konibo, are thinking of founding a new village.
Behind Pucallpa they have founded a large town.
They say that long ago the Spaniards founded the city of Lima.

s: Maníx kextó ikátiibira Otokoro jémake, jóni icha boxón ákana.
e: Many people went to found the community of Utucuro even though it had previously been dense forest.
In all plazas there are benches.

s: Jawen wái óroxonti ea yóiketianra en jén ake, koríki bikáskin.
e: When he told me I could farm his field, I agreed, because I wanted to earn money.

s: Jonín ríkanaitianronki aínbaonki nókoa iki, jéne meranoax joxón.
e: They say that while a man was casting his net, a woman came out of the water to meet him.
When father went to the oxbow lake (cocha), he came across a *yawámasen* bird.
This year the river's flood did not inundate our community.
They say that if we give a child sugarcane juice to drink, he becomes lazy.
chicken soup

s: Káchio kaxónra non jéne máanai méraa iki; ja jénera iká iki mátsi.
e: *Going into the monte (forest), we found a waterfall, and the water was cold.*

s: Jenén ewa benónronki non jemánkoki nócho ani pikóti iki.
e: They say that to signal a flood is coming, a large churo (a snail) will come out into our yard.

s: Nakáxonki, Jenén ewaítian jabáti kaí, tóoya aínbo iní iki.
e: They say the termite mound originated when a pregnant woman was fleeing from the Flood.
They say the *jenéntita* fish keeps the streams from drying up.

s: Non jenényawan ponyán síkaaronki nontín kaí noa íshto íti iki.
e: They say that when we rub our arms with an *esquila*, we can paddle faster.

s: Nato báritiabira jónibaon jaton pátoronbo moa jéneke.
e: This year the men have left their bosses.

s: Nato jóninra xóboakinbi jéneke, jawen báke wáiroron yatánketian.
e: This man was building a house, but he stopped doing it because his son was captured by the police.

s: Yóyoitibira rário jenéke, nato bakén masáaka.
e: The radio stopped working because this child broke it.

s: Awakanra níshi píaia moa jénetia íketian.
e: During flood season, the tapir eats vine-like grass.

s: Nato jénetianra jéne písi iántanke, manán réokootax.
e: During that winter, the water smelled bad because hills that had collapsed fell in.

s: Jénetiaketianra rébokiax páeri mawá toxbá pákeyantanke.
e: When there was a rise in the water, the current brought the corpse of a priest floating down from upriver.

s: Nokon títaiba mérati kanón kawe —ákara jén ike.
e: When she said to him, "Let's go for a walk to my mother's," he accepted.

s: Nato bákera ámakiri xenin ráchikiike; jáskatira jawen yóra jenkó iki.
e: This child spilled gamitana fish (gamitana) fat on himself; that's why his whole body smells rancid.

s: Xéni jenkó piáxa nato báke chíxotai.
e: Because he ate something with rancid oil, this child has diarrhea.

s: Ichayora xéni axónra nato xóntakon xée jenkóake.
e: By putting in too much oil, this girl made the fried food smell of pure oil.

s: Kabóri pexkan en xóiara jawen xéni jenkóke.
e: When I roasted the taricaya turtle (taricaya) shell, the fat took on a strong oily smell.

s: Moa xawén cháro jókonaitianronki jeó kéotai.
e: They say the *gualo* bird sings when the young of the charapa (river turtles) hatch.

s: Jépe pei bíi kaxónronki jonín wísoino rétenike.
e: They say that long ago a man killed a yanapuma (black puma) when he had gone to gather yarina leaves.

s: Yobébaonra noa óyokin jéshakai; noara isínhakai.
e: Sorcerers make a sucking noise when they suck on us, and it makes us hurt.

s: Xaén bóna píkoara jésikai; ja xaénra bóna píai.
e: The isula ant makes a "jes!" sound while the anteater pulls it out of its nest, and then it eats it.

s: Nato meósotira jesté iki; nokon awín betan senéma.
e: This ring is very narrow; it doesn't fit on my wife's finger.
This man made my shoe too narrow.

s: Jónironki manón jestéketian áni inón bínike.
e: They say a man was once attacked by a jaguar after getting stuck in the mud.
The girl was choked by the smell of something burning.

s: Osánhananbi átsapoto pikínra nato aínbaon jéteke.
e: This woman choked while eating fariña (toasted manioc flour), because she was laughing.

s: Nato báke yóitimanra máijexkon jawen wétsa tsákake.
e: This spoiled child deliberately hit his brother with a clod of earth.
This dog carried off a little piece of meat.

s: Nato simána jóaitonra nokon epán báke non koráka jíkimai.
e: Next week we will install my paternal uncle's son as curaca (village chief).

s: Moa kinimeran jíkia íketianra en píkoyamake.
e: I didn't take it out because it was already inside the hole.
My canoe got wedged under the launch's stern.

s: Tinínti jíkiaxa nato jóni siná banéke.
e: When he became lieutenant governor, this man became a despot.
On the left bank of the river the motor (outboard motor) sank.

s: Non ponyán jíma icha tékamaaronki ponkóxti iki.
e: They say that when we let many *jíma* ants bite our arm, we will gain vigor.
They say that if we drink a beverage mixed with *jímashia* ants, we become generous.
They say that if we eat something with a *jímashia* ant present, it can take away our stinginess.
They say the macaw *kabezón* is bright red because long ago it was painted with the blood of the Inca who had been killed.
My wife is one month pregnant.

s: Moa chónka rabé báritiaya ikaxa nato xóntako jímike.
e: At twelve years of age, this young woman menstruated.
The roasted gamitana (tambaqui fish) is undercooked at the tail.
to cut at the tail
boil on the penis
to wash the male parts of
They say that in Imiría men with tails once appeared
They say that long ago the *charapilla* carried off a man
The chimpanzee is a tailless monkey

s: Nato jóni yamín táxtetara jintá pánike.
e: When this man cut his foot with an axe, a blood clot stayed hanging in the cut

s: Non jínwachori píketianronki, non báke jímia chíxotai.
e: They say that if we eat the *lisa* fish, our little child gets bloody diarrhea

s: Jírafa jáke Ajírikain. Jawen níti iki keyá, téxo nenké.
e: The giraffe lives in Africa. It is very tall and has a very long neck.

s: Nato jóni jenén réteara máwatama iki; jíriapari riki.
e: This drowned man is not dead; he is still alive.

s: Piróta áakinra jonín máxkake; játianra ompáx jáki chikoxonres jíriakanke.
e: While playing soccer, a man fainted; then they threw water on him until they revived him.

s: Ronón nátexa máwatainbishokora rókotoron nato jóni jíriake.
e: The doctor saved the life of this man who was about to die from a snakebite.
They say God resurrected Jesus Christ.

s: Rabé báritia riki nato jonín yóra moa jírioma.
e: It has been two years for this man's body to be paralyzed.

s: Nato aínbaon kíshira jírioma iki; jáwekeska ikáxa jíriamai.
e: This woman's thigh has no feeling; perhaps it will not recover.

s: Bóchikiáx páketa bákera, jawen papán jírioma bóke.
e: The boy who fell from a height was carried by his father, lifeless.

s: Máwatáxbira nato aínbo jíriribike, rókotoron ráo xétemaa.
e: This woman was unconscious, but she revived when the doctor made her smell a medicine.

s: Abion pakéketianra westíora aínbobicho jíria iki.
e: A plane crashed and only one woman survived.

s: Kakónkonia jónira jiwín réteabi jírike, ráo xéamakana.
e: A man from Caco was crushed by a tree but revived when they made him drink medicine.

s: Nato néte sénenketianra noa jírinonxiki —akinra jóni máwatataton jawen báke áke, namá meranxon.
e: A deceased man told his son in a dream: —We will be resurrected at the end of the world.

s: Nato jónira kíkin yóashi iki itan jawen jisáribira jakómayora iki.
e: This man is truly wretched, and of very ugly appearance.

s: Nokon papán nóntira nato jónina jisákeskaribi iki.
e: My father's canoe looks exactly like this man's.

s: Papánra jawen bákebo paénxon oxá jishténhake.
e: The drunken father woke up his children while they were sleeping.
When the baby was crying, I woke up from my sleep.
They say that long ago the demon that causes whooping cough was quite visible.
They say the dead walk about at night, but they are invisible.

s: Westíora bákera jisís jawen pabíkiain jíkiax mawáke.
e: A boy died because an *ischimi* got into his ear.
Jesus Christ made a blind woman see.
Jesus Christ resurrected a dead person, something no one else could do.

s: Sarámpinin íkín jisón xéaaronki noa benxontiki.
e: They say that when someone has measles and drinks urine, they can be cured.

s: Ja chiraparonki ronín iki noki jísonai; jákopi ói béai.
e: They say the rainbow is a boa that urinates on us, and that is why the rain falls.

s: Pápa chopán mároara en jisá iki métsama; játian titánbiribi jisára jakón iki.
e: I see that the cloth papa bought is ugly, but mama sees it as pretty.

s: Ochó jóainbira en jíske jawéki papía jóaitian.
e: He was far away, but I saw that he was coming carrying the things.

s: Westíora yóximanronki jóni nókoxon yókata iki: ¿Minki néno jóni wínotai oínyamaa? Jánra nokon kabáyo bóke yómetsokin —akin aká iki. Játian yóia iki: Enra jisáma iki; westíora aínbobichoresa en oínke; ikáxbira kabáyooma íke —akin aká iki.
e: A certain demon met a man and asked him: —Haven't you seen a man pass by here? He stole my horse and took off with it. Then the man answered: —I haven't seen him. I only saw a woman, but she had no horse.
Although he was already as good as dead, the doctor revived him.

s: Róo bakera titán jiwéake, yamébobi xéamakin.
e: The mother raised a baby howler monkey so carefully that it didn't die; she even gave it something to drink at night.

s: Nato báke ísinai ikax óshishoko ikátiaira moa jiwéke jawen yóra moa
e: **bénxoax.** This child, who was so thin from having been sick for a long time, has recovered and is now healthy.

s: Nato joshínshino bakeshoko biára moa jiwéke; rámara ícha píai.
e: This baby pucahuapo (red uakari monkey) that I got from the forest has survived, and now it eats a lot.

s: Chósko pácha jíwira non xáteke; jánra non motórobo bíai.
e: We have cut down four hundred trees, with which we will buy motors (outboard boat motors).

s: Nétetiibira non jíwi pápiai pátoronin yónoa.
e: Every day we carry wood by order of the boss.
The boy died from falling out of the treetop.

s: Nato páena jónira yantán joí tatíipatanjoke.
e: This drunken man came stumbling along at dusk.
On my way back from the forest, I came along killing spider monkeys as I went.

s: Bíntiochotianronki non ískoira xobo joán raóati iki.
e: They say that for the 28th of July we should decorate the school with flowers.

s: Manánxaweronki noa nátexaxki wanín jóaketiampari xépishitiki
e: They say that when the tortoise bites us, it won't let go until the pijuayo (peach palm) flowers.

s: Jonín átsa jóaaronki yóshimanki píanana iki.
e: They say a demon ate the manioc that the man had boiled.

s: Nato paránta joára mératabo méniti iki.
e: This boiled plantain is for the visitors.

s: Káshibaon pía méetaxonki noa jóbo píkotai.
e: They say that if we touch the arrows of the Cashibo, a lump can appear on us.

s: Jawen jawéki jóboaxon bóaitianra, yómetsobaon jóni bichínke.
e: While a man was carrying his belongings wrapped in his clothing, thieves stole them from him.

s: Jónira wetsa nawabaon jawéki méetax jóboke.
e: The man touched things belonging to other tribes and developed a tumor.

s: Noa nanén tsákaaronki jóboti iki; jóboxonronki náne bimin xeyóti iki.
e: They say that if the huito fruit hits us, it raises a lump, and that the lump can be made to disappear by massaging it with the same fruit.

s: Westíora yósishokoronki jawen babánki jobóxkoki pián tsákaxon rétenike.
e: They say that long ago a little old man was killed by his grandson, who had shot him in the testicles with an arrow.

s: Jawen jochín jói ninkáxonyamaitianra nato báke jawen papán ríxkike.
e: When this child did not obey his older brother, his father whipped him.

s: Xawányainronki yamé joé píkotai jaton jémanapon.
e: They say that in Shahuaya, a light appears at night in people's yards.
My house has electric light.

s: Papánra rintírinaman jónibo joéake, tsóaborin ixon oínkaskin.
e: Dad shone the flashlight on the people to see who they were.
They say there was also a stone in the cave that shone.
I can't pronounce that word.

s: Aínbaonra Páokochankoxon Máioxiain jawen béneki jói ráanke, jawen pápa pishtákonin réteketian.
e: A woman sent a message to her husband from Paococha to Pucallpa, informing him that her father had been murdered by the pishtacos.

s: Inkán jónibaonronki non joínbi jato yóikatitai.
e: They say the Inca's messengers used to speak to them in our language.
His voice has broken into falsetto.
They say that giving sweet potato to a small child makes them stutter.

s: Nato jóninra join bismánhaxon mái tsákake.
e: This man lost his breath and fell to the ground.

s: Nato jenén rétea aínbaonra moa jóinai.
e: This woman who was drowning is breathing now.
They say the heart of the yacumama (mythical water-boa) is like a bass drum.
**maxonra sontari iti koáratianin yatánike.** A guard detained a certain man for military service without knowing that he was mute.

s: Ochítinin jojóakara báke íshtoi káke, natéxnaketian.
e: When the dog barked at him, the boy ran off, afraid it would bite him.

s: Nato ochítira yamé jojóishinai yómetsobo akí.
e: This dog has been barking all night at thieves.

s: Jókara jáke Asiain jainoax Nóriti Amírikain. Jara jáke jene meran. Jainoax maínribira níai, ikáxbi nikáskimai.
e: The seal lives in Asia and in North America. It lives in the water, but it also moves about on land, although with difficulty.

s: Nokon pátoroninra ea ronón ewa jókamake.
e: By order of my boss I skinned a large boa.

s: Moa joká ikénbira nato báke ínoki ráketai.
e: This child is afraid of the jaguar even though it is already skinned.
The teacher sent the students out to play.
The mother brought out her batch of clay prepared with charcoal from burnt apacharama bark.

s: Nato jónira jawen yóránko toxbábo jokónke.
e: This man broke out in blisters all over his body.
A herd of white-lipped peccaries has come out.

s: Westíora jóni máwatara jawen kéxakan jími jókona iki.
e: Blood came out of a dead man's mouth.

s: Sarámpi jokónxonra en yonáke, rabé néte.
e: When I broke out with measles, I had a fever for two days.
having hard testicles
to sew up the scrotum of
to pull out the pubic hair of

s: Jatíbi jawéki bíchira jonéshoko Máioshiain márokanai.
e: In Pucallpa they buy all kinds of hides clandestinely.

s: Non jawéki yóshiman jóneketianronki pikoshonon ichásh ránsati iki.
e: They say that when a demon hides something of ours, we have to dance so that it will bring it back to light.
Dad hid when his boss came.
They say a man once fought with the thunder demon.
The good man does not live on bread alone.

s: Jóni meránonronki náwashian kéotai non xóbo patáx.
e: They say that when the shihuango (an oropendola bird) sings near our house, it announces the arrival of visitors.
They say God is going to create a new earth.
They say that if we bury a deceased person wrapped in a blanket, he turns into a jaguar-man.
They say a demon carried off a child while he was playing at being an adult.

s: Rébokiaxa westíora jónikon nokóke, jawen tápaman.
e: A full-blooded Konibo arrived from the Upper Ucayali on his raft.

s: Ríosenra néte jónimaa iki, jawen kóshi shínaman.
e: God created the universe with his power.

s: Jóni réteaiboronki yobébaon óni xéaxon óinai jonín mápoxao téoya.
e: They say that sorcerers, upon drinking ayahuasca, see visions of murderers adorned with necklaces of human skulls.
We cannot, and never could, create ourselves.

s: Jóniwakaronki noa méraaxki wíniai non kaíbo iká ikax.
e: They say that if we were its relatives, neighbors, or countrymen, the ghost cow sheds tears upon seeing us.

s: Jónkanaxa nokon pápa bachín rakáke; chéxaa téneti átipanyamax.
e: My dad is lying in bed with a swollen testicle and he can no longer bear the pain.
A man was bitten by the collared peccary when it escaped after he had shot it.

s: Báritianra moa motóronin réboki bóyamakanai; jónoanaresa bókanai.
e: In the dry season it's difficult to go upriver by motor; one can only go by poling.

s: Jónira jawen jónoti sékebaini jéne meran káke; nónoti onámaiketianra jenén réteke.
e: When his punting pole broke, by chance, a man fell into the river and drowned because he didn't know how to swim.

s: Kirínkoninra jónxe sáwea íketian aínbo jóto tsékake.
e: A gringo took a photograph of a woman while she was wearing her cotton bracelets.

s: Westíora aínboronki jónxe áataitianki yóshiman téxtenike.
e: They say that while a woman was weaving cotton anklets, a demon beheaded her.
They say the female demon of the little *jóo* toad knows how to make good drink.
I undressed him even though he was embarrassed to take his clothes off.
Thieves took a man's shoes off.

s: Min chópa jópetabicho méraaxa noa íchabires wínike, mia inón biá shínanax.
e: We cried when we saw only the clothes you had taken off, because we thought a jaguar had attacked you.
jenén réteyamakeanke. If he had taken off his shoes, he wouldn't have drowned.

s: Nato pápashokonra moa jopóx mérati átipanyamake, moa yósishokoira íxon.
e: Grandpa can no longer see the isangüe mites because he is already too old.
Food produces semen.
They say the little *jóri* bird pecked into the gall bladder of Stingy Inca.

s: Moa kíshi jórina íshonra binán tékaabi onányamake.
e: He didn't notice when a wasp stung him because his thigh was already numb.

s: Nokon kíshira moa jorínke, nokon xaté ea raónxonyamakana.
e: My thigh has gone numb because they didn't treat the cut I had on it.

s: Papán chiárextira jóroya iki; épanabiribira jayáoma iki.
e: The pair of my father's pants has a lining, but my uncle's doesn't.
Greetings, friend.

s: Nokon pápa jótiiketianra paránta xoo kéntikan mápoxon en joshímake.
e: Since my father was about to arrive, I ripened some green plantains by covering them inside a pot.
Mom's pampanilla (wraparound skirt) is cinnamon-colored.
This child is crying because he wants to drink ripe plantain drink.

s: Nato aínbaonra jawen chitónti joshínhake, wísoati shinánkin.
e: This woman dyed her pampanilla cinnamon-colored while trying to dye it black.

s: —Pápara weánrebon káa iki, xóboanoxon joshínjiwi bénai.
e: Dad went to the headwaters of the stream looking for dragon's blood trees for building the house.

s: Joshínjiwironki jími boánkin xéaa jakón iki.
e: They say it is good to drink infusions of dragon's blood when one has bleeding.

s: Nato bákera binán tékaa joshínkiranke wínikasi.
e: This child turned red, about to cry, because a wasp had stung him.

s: Paránta moa joshínketianra nokon títa en kénamake kókoi jonón ixon.
e: When the bananas had ripened, I sent for my mother to come taste them.

s: Non jóso yatánketianronki noa xenón átiki.
e: They say that if we catch a *jóso* moth with our hand, it can give us scabies.
pot, water, matches, and firewood
