to look backward
to spill (several things) below a container
Watch out, the snake will bite you.

s: Jawen báke ábionin kánaketian aínbaon yóiabira; káke, yóitima ikáx.
e: The mother fearfully advised her son not to go in the small airplane, but he stubbornly went anyway.

s: Aweitianin káyamawe —akinra nokon báke en áke káxibobaon rétenaketian.
e: I told my son not to go to the Aguaytía river, fearing that the Cashibo would kill him.

s: Nokon titánra jawen pói pakénaketian yóiabi, ninkáxonyamax páketi tobíke.
e: Although my mother told her brother to be careful not to fall, he paid no attention; he fell and got hurt.
It's my brother's.

s: Ono riki non átapa. Nokon títanatoninra píai.
e: There are our hens. The one that's eating is my mother's.

s: Néno riki ícha ochíti: Josíkanatonra ea natéxke.
e: There are many dogs around here; José's bit me.
my, mine
your (familiar or formal), yours
his/her, his/hers
our, ours
your (plural), yours (plural)
their, theirs

s: —¿Mínarin nato rirós? —Jeje, nókona riki. Ichabires iráke.
e: —Is this watch yours? —Yes, it's mine. Thank you very much.
Nónabaonra kánánai. They are playing soccer. Ours are winning.
The child killed a snake in its nest.

s: Binán naa jonín xobónkoxon ménoaronki ja xóbo ibo jábatai.
e: They say that if a wasp's nest burns in a house, the owner moves away.
The little birds have eaten my rice (to my detriment).
He has killed my dog (to my detriment).
He has taken my dog away.
He brought it and it harmed me.
He brought it in order to harm me.

s: Westíora aínbo yoxínbakenra jawen bákebi nabákanin cháchixon réteke.
e: A certain crazy woman killed her own child with a penknife.
I covered the floor of the boat with boards.

s: Nato xóbora bebíori jakómashoko jisá iki; ikáxbi, jawen nabíorira jakónshamanki.
e: This house looks ugly on the outside, but on the inside it's very pretty.

s: Nato Yarínainoa jonínra nabíro xéwati onányamake.
e: This man from Yarinacocha doesn't know how to weave *nabíro*-type baskets.

s: Nato parónra íchayora nabón iki; jáskara kopira, ícharibi isínkanai.
e: Along the Ucayali there are many shingutos, and that's why many people get sick.
Good morning, aunt Méa.

s: Nokon náchi Rimán kayántanara moa kímisha báritia iki, ráma kamanbi joáma.
e: It has already been three years since my aunt went to Lima, and to this day she hasn't turned up.

s: Nato jonínra jawen náchi yóyoakai, non áshekan jaskáatima ikénbi.
e: This man converses with his mother-in-law, although this is not permitted in our custom.
Pour it into the bottle.

s: Naíronki níi iki; ochóira ikax yankón.
e: They say the sky is a forest, and since it's so far away, it's blue.
to the sky

s: Náto báke tárora náka íchaya iki; ikáxbi náshikashamai.
e: This dirty boy is covered in gnats, but he doesn't want to bathe.
This boy cut himself with a machete.

s: Kóchi nami nákati shinánkinra, aínbaon jawen bákeres méxteke.
e: A woman cut off her son's hand while trying to cut pork meat.

s: Nato jonínra nákaxomabi píai; jákopira pokón chéxai.
e: This man eats without chewing, and that's why he has a stomachache.

s: Jatíribi jónibaonra nakáx píai, já píti yámaketian.
e: Some people eat termites for lack of food.
Termites are used as medicine.

s: Nakáxonki, jenén ewaitian jabáti kaí, tóoya aínbo iní iki.
e: They say the termite mound originated when a pregnant woman fled the flood.

s: Noa yóyoikaitianra nakáxen noa ákai máwakin, jóni keskaribi saí ikin.
e: If we speak, the termite mound answers us like an echo, and cries like those of a person are heard.
The drunk man is lying in the muddy mud.

s: Nokon táera, min máno meran nakómake.
e: You put my feet in the mud.

s: Páena jonínra jawen taén máno nákoke.
e: The drunk man put his feet in the mud.

s: Nokon bákera manón nákotax sión iitai.
e: My son screams because his feet are stuck in the mud.

s: Namá meranronki yóshiman meráya ráo méniai.
e: They say that the demon gives medicine to the healer in his dream.

s: Bákebora namán tsínikanai; jato jenémawe irai tita.
e: The mother says: "The children are playing down below; tell them to stop playing."
A dog that was underneath the seat bit me.
There are some lizards lying at the foot of the ravine.

s: Piróta ákai bebónbires íkasira nokon chái namánbires íke.
e: My brother-in-law ended up last because he wanted to be first at soccer.

s: Nokon titánra jawen átapa, ríkaton namánbires máromake.
e: My mother sold her hen to a trader at a very low price.

s: Nokon wétsara namánbires shinánya nénoa jóni iki.
e: My brother is the least intelligent man around here.
I had a nightmare last night.
I've already gotten tired of eating meat.

s: Moatianronki náne bíi kaxón jonín áni íno méranike, jáki jóaitian.
e: Very many years ago a man went to get huito in the forest and came across an enormous jaguar coming toward him.

s: Páenax jokáshamainbira jonín jawen wétsa nontín nánexon béke.
e: A man who was drunk didn't want to come, but his brother loaded him into a canoe and brought him.

s: Nokon machíto nánea ikénbira, papán bénabenai.
e: Even though my machete is already loaded (on the boat), my father keeps looking for it.

s: Koríki yómetsoxonra jonín jawen bórosa meran náneke.
e: The man put the money in his bag after he stole it.

s: Titánra jawen báke jaín nánetinin náneke.
e: The mother rocked her baby in a cradle.

s: Nato aínbora jawen bakénaneti sóoika iki.
e: This woman's womb has become swollen.
The man boarded a boat headed for Iquitos.
They say that when a child is cutipado (spiritually contaminated) by a huapo monkey, he gets dysentery.
When building the house, I made it crooked because I'm not an expert.

s: Níweaba koshin xóbo nantánketianra moa rásakanke.
e: They tore down the house because a strong gust of wind bent it.

s: Moa bími íchayora ikaxa nato kaímito jiwi moa nantáke.
e: This caimito (star apple) tree has bent over because it has too much fruit.

s: Nato isónxoma jíwira nantá iki; jáskatira tsóabi ján néeyamai pakénaketian.
e: This sapote tree is crooked, and that's why no one climbs it, for fear of falling.
Termites eat the inner part of the catahua tree.

s: Nato nónti máxkoshoko ikénbira jónibo íchayora nápokooke.
e: Although the canoe was very small, a great many people boarded it.

s: En tasá jenénko áketianra, ícha sipán nápokooke.
e: When I put the basket in the water, many sardines got into it.

s: Nato aínbaon bákera jawen nápomeameken yámake.
e: This woman's son doesn't have a middle finger.
Don't go to the middle of the river.

s: Aniwaporora páro napon réokooke sámaman ímaa.
e: A steamship sank in the middle of the river because of a whirlpool.
In Caco small planes land in the middle of the street.
ten and a half
The flag is white in the middle.

s: Moa napónketianra nónti non bíti átipanyamake, jatíbi nónoti onámabo ixon.
e: When the canoe drifted to the middle of the river, we couldn't recover it because none of us knew how to swim.
They loaded many things onto the boat.

s: Jawen bakén parántajoshinbo chómo meran napóketianra, titán bénabenai.
e: The mother keeps looking for the ripe plantains because her son put them in a large jar.

s: Jíwi nichínoxon papán mái chínia ikénbi titán mái napóketianra papán sináake.
e: Papa scolded mama because she put dirt in the hole he had dug to set some posts.

s: Naránxa xoo kókoaxa nato báke jánshoke.
e: This child has patco (a stomach ailment) because he ate a green orange.

s: Jawen báke, aínbaon náshimaketianra, rókotoron notsínke, ísinai ikénbi ímaketian.
e: The woman bathed her little son while he was still sick, and the doctor scolded her for it.

s: Rabé néte náshiama ikax, tsókasira ea moa náshike.
e: Since it had been two days since I hadn't bathed, I felt annoyed, so I bathed.

s: Moa náshia ikénbira, nato báke jákiribi náshimakanai.
e: Even though this boy already bathed, they're bathing him again.
We were baptized in the river.

s: Ján níninakinra bákebaon nokon risbí nashíke.
e: Since the children were tugging at my rope in a struggle, it broke.

s: Nato risbí nashíra bákebaon bóke ján tsíniti.
e: The children took this broken rope away to play with it.
Papa found a dead snake on the river island.

s: Parónra moa nási íchayora iki, jénetiaibatax.
e: Many islands have formed in the river after the water rose.

s: Píshara pékeya ikáx nasí ike jawékia.
e: The bag that was carrying things emptied out because it had a hole.

s: Násimaxkainra xóno tapan rásike; jatíbi jónira jenén jato kéyokeanke.
e: The lupuna (kapok-wood) raft broke apart at the upstream tip of the island, and everyone nearly drowned.
I'm cleaning the pot on the inside.
, jonín wísoino méraxon rétea iqui. While following a trail looking for a tapir, a man came across a black jaguar and killed it.

s: Maístoronra báke jóniati onán shínanai, natánxon áketianres.
e: The teacher thinks his student knows how to draw, but he's only tracing.

s: Xóbo natapotinimeaxa báke pakéke; ikáxbi mawáyamake.
e: A child fell from a crossbeam of the house, but did not die.
I spilled all the food on the ground.
While cooking the rice, it stuck to the inside of the pot.
An isula (bullet ant) stung me where the child had bitten me.
This bitten plantain is already rotting.

s: Westíora aínbo ísinaironki jána nátexbaini mawáke.
e: They say a sick woman died biting her own tongue.
That snake is venomous.

s: Westíora jonínra, paénxon jawen pápa na
e: téxon réteke. A drunk man killed his father by biting him.
The house filled up with smoke when they burned the garden plot.
The sky filled up with clouds.

s: Náto átapa benenra átapa awin xéki píanaanai.
e: This rooster is eating the hen's corn.
We have never seen this man.
That brother in Christ is pure of heart.

s: Náto yóikinra en mia áatai; jábira min ninkáyamake —akinra ea maístoron áke.
e: The teacher told me: "I was referring to this one, but you didn't understand me."

s: Náto betanra ea ochó kái —akinra ea aínbaon yóibake.
e: "I will go far away with him," the woman told me.

s: Pián natsákinra jawen táeres jonín cháchike.
e: The man accidentally speared his own foot with an arrow.

s: Jonínronki pián táe cháchike, ikáxbironki ishtón tsékake jenemeranoa.
e: They say a man speared his foot with an arrow, and then quickly pulled it out of the water.
Did you drink all the water without leaving any?

s: Náwabaon kónxaman téetaibo yamé kéyoara; jatíribishokores jabákana iki.
e: Some wild Indians killed the loggers at night; only a few escaped.
Now some mestizos want to live in Caco, among us.
They say that long ago our ancestors used to flee out of fear of white people.

s: Westíora jónira ikai néskati: Náwabaonra jato xéni tsékai.
e: A man says the following: "Foreigners (who are pishtacos) extract people's fat."

s: Inkánronki jawen rayós pián náwaaka, manxánteonike.
e: They say that when the Inca shot his arrow at his son-in-law, the latter turned into a manshaco.

s: Nokon nawánjane riki Hiliador Dávila Rengifo.
e: My name in Spanish is Hiliador Dávila Rengifo.

s: Ja jóni yósira nawé bira iki.
e: An old man may be stooped.

s: Nato páan játiobi ikáxbira chichó náxaa iki.
e: This bread, which appears whole, is hollow inside.

s: Westíora bákera naxánkenin káx mawákeanke; itíbira jawen títán méraxon bíke.
e: A child nearly died after falling into a hole; when he was about to die, his mother found him and saved him.
The oranges that mother mother brought are dried out (without juice).

s: Nato santíra rákatara moa náxaa iki.
e: This watermelon lying on the ground is hollow inside.
The Ucayali River is wide.
its width

s: Yaŕina baira moa náxbáakanke, jakón íti akin.
e: They have widened the road to Yarina to make it better.

s: Báritiatiibira non páro náxbatai, kétokan ímaa.
e: Every year the Ucayali River widens because of landslides.
The corpse of the man who died from lack of appetite has a sunken stomach.

s: Rimán boxón ráo xéamakanara nato jóni xóata iki; jáinoax joaxa moa jákiribi náxpeke ráo xéayamai.
e: This man was taken to Lima, made to take medicines, and he gained weight. When he returned he lost weight again because he wasn't taking the medicines.

s: Níwaman ompáx nayáaitianra jéne potá jókonai.
e: When the water is shaken by an earthquake, it turns murky.

s: Jéne meranoáx pikókirankironki róniman jéne nayáakai.
e: They say that when the yacumama (mythical water-boa) comes out of the water, it shakes the water off its body.

s: —¿Jáweranoki Péna káa? —Káama riki. Oa xóbo chicho náyakaa riki.
e: "Where did Pena go?" "She hasn't gone anywhere. She's sitting inside that house."
Sit the child inside the hammock.

s: Jéne náyataitianronki yoxánshokon sión ishon máxkaa iki.
e: They say that when the river water shook, an old woman screamed and fainted.
to throw oneself into the water
to put into the water

s: Tapíchinin kaxónra, néa kéotai keskati inábo íkai
e: en nínkata iqui. When I went to the Tapiche river, I heard the savages imitating the trumpeter's call.

s: Jatíbi xóbo neabora moa nákaxen píke.
e: The termites have eaten all the house's bindings.

s: Níbue koshinra en jíwi néaa moa xákaake.
e: The strong wind has loosened the poles I tied.

s: Ronón ewanronki, awá néaa iki, ompáx xeaitian.
e: They say the boa coiled around the tapir while it was drinking water.

s: Kobínhawe nato tsismán betan bóe; moa kobínketian boé nebíwe.
e: Boil the fasaco and the boquichico fish, and when it's boiled, take out the boquichico.
They say a woman turned into a termite mound because she couldn't climb a tree.
I got stained with mud.

s: Neíno jáke Orópain jaínoax Nóriti Amírikain. Ja riki áni jaínoax siná ochíti keska.
e: The wolf lives in Europe and North America. It is like a large, fierce dog.

s: Nékea baínra móxa ícha iki; jaó káyamawe —akínra ea yóikanke, ea káchio káitian.
e: When I was going to the forest, they told me: "On this side of the path there are many thorns; don't go that way."
4 plus 4 equals 8.

s: Nato páro riki, jénetian kikínbires nemín; ikáxbiri iki, báritianbiribi benéshoko.
e: The Ucayali is very deep in the rainy season, but in the dry season, on the contrary, it has very little water.

s: Manánkini nemínhainoax yoxín jóxonronki jóni píti piánike.
e: They say that long ago a demon came out of a deep cave and ate a man's food.

s: Pósora moa non nemínhake, jéne íchama íketian; rámara moa jéne ícha iki.
e: We deepened the well because there wasn't enough water; but now there's plenty.

s: Jéne béketianra moa Yarína ian nemínke.
e: Lake Yarina has deepened due to the rise in water.

s: Chomómea ompáxa bakóxa iki, bakén jabón nénana.
e: Foam has formed in the water jar because a child put soap in it.

s: Ompáxa táshi méskoxon síkaaronki néne jénetai.
e: They say the pain of a burn eases when salt water is poured on it.

s: Jawen nenéronki ténetimayora iki —ikira jóni íkai.
e: The man says the pain of his burn is unbearable.

s: Nokon menóra rímoman axón min néneake.
e: When you poured lemon on my burn, you made me feel pain.

s: Bitániainoa jonínronki jína nenké jóni mérake.
e: They say a man from Betania saw a man with a long tail.

s: Komán jíwi riki, jatíbi jíwi bebon nenkéyora.
e: The shihuahuaco is the tallest of all the trees.

s: Ja jonín jínaronki ike jawen nenké westíora mítorobira.
e: They say that man's tail was more or less a meter long.

s: Kómaman yoshínronki xobón keyátio iki jawen nenké.
e: They say the demon of the shihuahuaco tree is as tall as a house.
They have lengthened the Caco airfield.

s: Papánra jawen xóbo moa nenkéake, jíbui ícha axón.
e: Papa made his house longer by adding more wood.
I want a short board.

s: Papán chiárextira máxko biábi pátsata nenkéke.
e: The small pair of pants papa bought stretched when washed.

s: Nénora rabé aínbo winókainke; jára íbirai yatánoxon bénakanai.
e: Two women have passed by here; they are possibly the ones being sought to be caught.
He isn't here.

s: Yaméra rabé yómetso joni néno jowánke; jóketianra yatáwankanke.
e: Last night two thieves came here, and when they came, they were caught.
I am from here.
He left from here.
The cortadera grass cut me.
The tuquituqui (jacana) doesn't sink when walking on the guama (leaves/branches).
Mother put the aguaje fruit in a pot of water.
Nima, come here.

s: Noa néria jónibora onán iki —ikira Sán Rantsísko jónibo yóyo íkai iki, rébokiabo onámanin yóini.
e: The people of San Francisco say: "We who live in this place are cultured." And in this way they claim that the people upriver are uncultured.

s: Nato óiki rakéyamawe; moa neséa riki; miara mecháyamai.
e: Don't be afraid of this rain. It has already calmed down, and you won't get wet.
The masato is right at a middle point: between fermented and sweet.
The rain has already calmed down.

s: Moa bechón néseketianra noa jóke; jákopira noa réokooyamake.
e: We came when the waves had already calmed down, and that's why we didn't capsize.

s: Enra nóntiakin neskáakin ákai; minra wétsaresibiaxon ákai.
e: I make the canoe this way, while you make it another way at the same time.

s: Jonínra ea áke neskáakin: —Nokon niskán Xéawe mia rayá inon —akin.
e: A man said the following to me: "Drink my sweat so that you become a strong worker."
We must grab it this way.
We must go this way.
A day has 24 hours.

s: Amakiriainoa bintístabaonra, tomínko neténbi jato téeti yóiai.
e: The Adventists of Amaquiría are made to work on Sundays.

s: Moa néte keyóti ochómaxokoronki áni káxibo benónxiki.
e: They say that when the end of the world comes, large bats will surely come.

s: Jawen netén káxa, moa kirínkobo béyamanonxiki.
e: If the foreigners go to their own country, they will not return.

s: Inka joxónronki non néte jakón ímanoxiki.
e: They say that when the Inca returns, he will improve our lives.
wild goose

s: Yaméra noa káchio káa iki; káxa moa néte xabáaketian noa íaman nókota iki.
e: At night we went to the forest, and by the time it was dawning we arrived at the lake.
Since the day has turned out so nice, we are working.

s: Jabuéki yókatabi netéketianra maístoron báke ríxkike.
e: The teacher hit a student because he stayed quiet when asked a question.

s: Sontáro káxbbi, netéxoko ítainra ja jamákanai.
e: If one goes into military service and is quiet, they kick him.

s: Yómetsoninra nónti bóyamake, jawen nexá oínxon.
e: The thief didn't take the canoe when he saw how it was tied.

s: Ké-tokanra nónti bóyamake moa en néxakona íketian.
e: The landslide didn't take the canoe because I had tied it well.

s: Sapén cháchiaxbi rísbikan nexéketianra jóni sápeman bónike.
e: Long ago a man was carried off by a manatee he himself had harpooned, because he got tangled in the harpoon line.

s: Moa píti yámaketianra ráma nexnéxbobi píkanai.
e: Since food is scarce these days, things like hoatzin are eaten.

s: Kónxaman téetaiboronki néte xabáti ochóma yábuakanike; westíora jónires íamanike yóiti ikáx.
e: They say that long ago some loggers turned into white-lipped peccaries at dawn, and only one was saved for being obedient.
that becomes a bird
I am from Caco.
I have come from Caco.

s: Non rekénboronki móxa meran níakaatax mawápaonike.
e: They say our ancestors used to die when they got into thorny places.

s: Titán koríkira en moa bonánti chicho níake.
e: I have already put mom's money away in the trunk.

s: Maríta meran koríki niá ikénbira, ea yómetsoakana en shinánke.
e: The money was tucked away in the suitcase, but I thought it had been stolen from me.
They say that if a baby is exposed to the night dampness it gets sick with patco.
The scorpion's sting is very painful.
They say the scorpion and the spider insult each other.

s: Ninbón cháironki bóna iki; jákopira jáweayamai.
e: They say the scorpion's brother-in-law is the isula (a stinging ant) and that is why it doesn't harm him.
After sweeping, the woman piled up the trash.

s: Níbopotatiainoa jakóma jawékiaira nato báke ísinke.
e: This boy got sick from eating spoiled things from the garbage dump.

s: Jíwi réraabira poxóyamax níchimeeke; níchimeetaxa jaínbi tánoke.
e: The tree I cut down fell, got stuck in the ground, and dried up there.

s: Xoboanoxon jíwi nichínkanara niwén jato póxanaanke.
e: The posts that were planted to build the house were knocked down by the wind.

s: Aínbaonra jawen báke chíikan nichínke, paénxon.
e: A drunk woman made her little child stand in the fire.

s: Nokon jíwi nichinra ea tsékanaanxon potánkana iki.
e: The stick I planted, they pulled out and threw away.

s: Nokon cháira jawen báke betanbicho níi meran benóke.
e: My brother-in-law and one of his children got lost walking alone in the forest.
wild animal

s: Enra awá tóoakinbi réteyamaa iki, níimaxo píaitian.
e: I shot at the tapir while it was eating tender plants, but I didn't kill it.
not to worry about what one will eat nor what one will wear
dog: The dog bit the child.

s: Sán Rantsískoainronki moa rérakana ikaxbi jíwi nínake janbíx.
e: They say that in San Francisco a tree stood back up again, even though it had fallen.

s: Nato jóni nínaa íketianra jatíribibaon osánke.
e: When the man was standing, the others laughed at him.
My little son started to walk for the first time just as a windstorm was coming.

s: Nokon kéen riki tsínikin jato níniti.
e: What I like is to play pulling on a rope and dragging everyone along.
The whirlpool pulled the boat.

s: Motóro rónikai en ninkákenbira, nato yosín ninkáyamake, pábe ixon.
e: I heard the noise of the motor, but that old man didn't hear anything because he is deaf.

s: Moa maton nínkata íketianra, ea Rimán kátana en mato yóiamai.
e: I'm not going to tell you any more about my trip to Lima because you have already heard it.

s: Nawán join kírika yóyo akinra en ninkáyamai; nón joinbi akínresa en nínkatai.
e: When I read something in Spanish, I don't understand; but in our own language, I do.
I don't understand you.

s: Maton ninká jawékira en moa mato yóikashamai.
e: I don't want to repeat again what you have already understood.

s: Enpachora éseai; jabira ea jói ninkáxonyamai.
e: I'm always the one who advises him, but he doesn't pay attention to me.

s: Manón nínoti kakáskimaitianra jóni inón bíke.
e: A man slipped in the mud, and while he was struggling to move, a jaguar attacked him.

s: Nato bakén kotón onara nisáira iki.
e: This child's patched shirt has many tatters hanging from it.

s: Tapán néxanoxon níshi bénai kaxa jóni níi meran benóke.
e: A man went to the forest to look for vines to tie up the raft, and got lost.

s: Awakanra níshi píai moa jénetia íketian.
e: When it is rainy season, the tapir eats climbing plants.
The healers who drank ayahuasca sang all night.

s: Níi meranra níshno tóoati pishíke, jaín jóni káama ikaxbi.
e: A gunshot was faintly heard far off in the forest, even though no one had gone there.
I could barely hear it thundering far off.

s: Máioshiainoax ábion nóyaara jawen rón moa níshnoke.
e: The sound of the plane flying from Pucallpa gradually faded away.

s: Níshoboronki moátian jápaonike; jaton tepón ícha ípaonike.
e: They say that long ago the *nísho* people used to set many traps along their trails.

s: Jonínra áke ea neskáakin: —Nokon niskán xéawe mia rayá inon —akin.
e: A man said this to me: —Drink my sweat so that you become a strong worker.
The skin has pores.
I stood up, and my body hurt.

s: Nato jónira íshtomashoko níai rókotoron xátea ikax.
e: This man walks slowly because the doctor operated on him.

s: Jáboman chókitaxa noa jáskatax íti iki, jakónyonax níi.
e: We wash with soap so we can go about well groomed.

s: Nítikoma jónira Rimán bokánke, jawen táe moa xátenoxon.
e: They took a lame man to Lima to have his foot amputated.
lame from birth
This man weeps bitterly because he became lame.

s: Ríma ochómaika jémameabora níwaman jaton xóbo rásakanke.
e: The houses of the residents who live near Lima were destroyed by an earthquake.
When the earthquake happened, the children fell to the ground.
They say the spirit of the wind has great power to blow.

s: Níwe xéaaxa westíora báke ésteax mawáke.
e: A certain boy inhaled a toxic gas; his stomach swelled up and he died.
They say that in a future war the foreigners will surely poison the air.

s: Mayániwenra jato kinámati átipanke, játoki pakéxon.
e: A small whirlwind, when it catches people, can make them vomit.

s: Níweabatamapari ikénra noa jóke; jákopira noa jakónbires nokóke.
e: We came before the windstorm rose, and that is why we arrived safely.

s: Nato nétera moa jakónhira iki, ói béyamaitian níweshaman ikax.
e: Today is a good day; it isn't raining and there is a breeze.
to cut at the navel
boil
to insert (something pointed) toward the inside

s: Nóabora moa apón ónanabo iki —ikira San Rantsísko jónibo íkai.
e: The people of San Francisco say: —We are now recognized by the government.

s: Yáminawabora nóki sinákanike, non jaton kaíbobo rétea shínanax.
e: The Yaminahua got angry with us because they thought we had killed their people.

s: Rámaronki non Inka noa ícha jawéki rikárani joai.
e: They say that now our Inca is coming to give us many gifts.

s: Bakénra jawen wétsa pián nóake, pokónko.
e: A boy jabbed his little brother's belly with an arrow.
**nonbex yóyo ikai ipaonike, non Ínka néno janóntian.** They say that long ago the dove used to talk, back when our *Inca lived around here.
The *tarahui likes eating *nócho snails very much.
They say that when a child is *cutipado (magically affected) by a *nócho snail, he gets bloody diarrhea.
Since the bread is very tasty, the child wants to eat it.
The meat of the *paiche (giant fish) is delicious.
She seasoned the *paiche porridge with onion.

s: Titán pítiaara moa yóchi aká nóeke.
e: The food that mother prepared has become tasty because she added chili pepper.

s: Kabóri noi xoiresara nato jóni píkasai.

I deflated the ball by squeezing it.
My mother is milking the cow.

s: Nato báke ésteara janbíx pótsitai, níwe jokónhakasi.
e: This child with a bloated belly squeezes himself to force the air out of his stomach.
The milk cow is milked every day.
The dog bit me when someone knocked me down.
Dad felled the lupuna tree in two days.

s: Jiwi poxá ikáinra ochíti siná iki.
e: Where the fallen tree is, there is a fierce dog.
Children are forbidden to eat the *póxko* type of shirúe so that it doesn't give them diarrhea.
I fell when I stepped on the ball.
They say strong men's arms are very muscular.

s: Shankón bíaitianra jóni jabuen póyaman réteke.
e: The branch of the uvilla (a tree grape) fell and killed the man while he was gathering its fruit.
to bruise on the body
to wash on the outside
I'm already going.
–Did your mother go upriver? –Yes; she went.
He is my father.

s: Onibirisitaro átira nokon báke en Rimán ráanke.
e: I sent my son to Lima to do university studies.

s: Píkeronra jawen báke jéne meran ráanke.
e: Pedro let his son fall into the water.

s: Epán yórara moa barín iki ráaxeke.
e: My uncle's body is already getting used to the sunny climate.

s: Eara átapa rábekan kéenai; mónsora kéenai rábe ochítibaken.
e: I want two hens, and at the same time the mestizo wants two puppies.
Before, about three years ago, there were indeed palm-thatch houses in Pucallpa, but now there are none.

s: Píkerora jawen pápa betan rábetai jóni tímakasi.
e: Pedro and his father stay close together because a man wants to hit him.
Four is an even number.

e: Antonio boasts because he knows how to read and knows big cities.
I don't boast about myself.
It is shameful for us to be found out that we have stolen something.

s: Tomás riki rabín joni; aínbo keska.
e: Tomás is a shy man; like a woman.
A shameless man robbed me.

s: Nokon nónti jakóma íketianra ea rabínke.
e: I have been ashamed of my canoe because it is poorly made.
I am shy before Tomás; that's why you go alone.
We worship God.
Mother praised my sister for her beauty.
**kanai.** They praise Sheca's nephew for his skill at fishing.
Let's nail the board with the nails.
You have a big knee.
My uncle, my maternal aunt's husband, tames wasps.
The shaman tames terrible demons.

s: En yáwa báke biára ráeke ishtónbires.
e: The baby huangana (white-lipped peccary) I caught has become tame very quickly.

s: Moátianra ípaonike áni jemánkobo ráibo jaí.
e: Long ago there were kings in the big towns.

s: Enra wáme cháchikin raínshake, yópa ixon.
e: When I speared a paiche (arapaima), I let it slip because I'm clumsy at fishing.

s: Westíora xóntakonra jawen ránboxo bishkóke raínshikin.
e: A certain young lady, slipping, fell on her knees and scraped them.
The man checks himself over after getting dressed.
The woman made her little son lie down.

s: Eara yoná akí báchi meran rakáke.
e: I am lying in the mosquito net with a fever.
A big lagarto (caiman) is lying far off there.

s: Jóni ísinaira rakátinin ápake kana iki.
e: They brought the sick man down on a stretcher.
I wrap my little son in a cloth.
They say our ancestors were a fearful people.

s: Mía riki raké; éa riki rakéma.
e: You are a coward; I am brave.
The jaguar frightened me.

s: Titánra nokon wétsa rakéake, ráo xéanon ixon.
e: Mother threatened my little brother so he would take the medicine.
Because we are real men, we are not afraid of anyone.
I am afraid of my enemy.

s: Rákexto paróyariki kája keska: jatíbi jawen paróbo senénbires.
e: A cube is like a box, and all its sides are equal.
This fearless man is following the fierce dog.
The girl wrapped the doll in a cloth.
I brought the cloths already wrapped.
My grandmother covers herself with the blanket when she is cold.
Cover that pihuicho (parrot chick) with the blanket.
Now our fellow countrymen no longer work with rubber.
Today I am going to Pucallpa.

s: — ¿Jáwetian mia Ikítoainoax joárin? —Ramáma ea joní riki.
e: —When did you come from Iquitos? —I came years ago.
Papa twists the vine.
Falling onto the fire, the girl burned her body badly.
Pedro, you are bad.
I ruined my boss's motorbike.
My wife treats me very badly.

s: En wishaa iki chónka jói. Kímisha en rámia iki.
e: I wrote ten words, and I made mistakes in three.
The boy cursed his companion.
*The airplane broke down in flight.*
Ana has become mean toward her companion.
Go get medicine; I've cut my foot with the hoe.
Bring the lamp over here.
Light the oil lamp because it's very dark.
The back of your knee is very dirty.
for one's knee to become less swollen
not hiding anything
They say our ancestors used to flip charapas (river turtles) over to catch them.

s: Nokon bótira ranbéke, béchoman ompáx bóchoaka.
e: My boat capsized because the wave filled it with water.

s: Nokon bákera moa ránbetai píchika óxeyanix.
e: My son already rolls over at five months of age.
A rectangle has unequal sides.
Papa has thick hair on his arms.
Pigs have bristles.
Sheep's wool is used to make cloth.

s: Bakénra átapa rani ménoke yóitima ixon; ménoxonra já píke.
e: The boy burned a hen's feathers because he's very mischievous, and after burning them he ate them.

s: Eara ránomis iki; nokon awínra en ránoai.
e: I am jealous; I feel jealousy over my wife.
Juan feels jealous over his wife.
Pedro is going to dance.
My kneecap hurts; rub it for me.
My father snores when he sleeps.
Go get plant medicine to cure Moisés.
There are many medicines at the pharmacy.
The bite of the loro machaco (a venomous snake) has no antidote.
The woman decorates her house for the party.
A man poisoned himself.
The herbalist woman kills people.
The health worker gave pills to my sick son.
The woman poisoned her rival.

s: Nokon papánra wéxati ráonai, jawen rawí wéxaa mawánon ixon.
e: My father is applying poison to his ushate (machete) so that his enemy will die when he cuts him on the neck.
The woman put on her adornments to go for a walk.
My mother's adornments are many.
Your baby was born with a half-white skin tone.
This man has plant medicines.

s: Papánra ochíti rapésteke chíkiri néeketian jawen píshpachiain.
e: Papa sheared the dog because gum had stuck to its side.
They say that long ago the friars taught our ancestors to build sugar-cane presses.

s: Nokon papán rapíchi. Rapíchininra non xáwi móxai.
e: This is my father's sugar-cane press. The cane is ground with the press.
Mama, I want a pencil.

s: Bixón óina tóo ati moa rápoia íketianra, en pótaibake.
e: When I picked up the shotgun, I saw it was already rusted, and I threw it away.
Our relatives love us.

s: Misionirobora jaton rárebo jénebeirani Piróri békana iki.
e: The missionaries came to Peru leaving their relatives behind.

s: Noa jábo betan ráenanai ikax iki misionirobo non rárebokeska; Ríosen janénko non rárebo.
e: Since we have become friends with the missionaries, they are our friends; in other words, our relatives in the name of God.

s: Senényoin jawen rárionin noa Sankénbea béwaitian ninkámaara, onís iki.
e: When Senényoi played Sankénbea for us on his tape recorder, it was nostalgic.

s: Jawen báke Rimámeax nokóketianra, títa rároke.
e: When her son arrived from Lima, the mother was glad.

s: Rásaro isinra néno yámatanike; Ajírika jemánres ícha jónibo rásaroya iki.
e: Leprosy barely exists around here; in Africa, though, there are many people with leprosy.

s: Joán riki rásaroya; ochó ráankanwe jáinoax mawánon.
e: Juan is a leper; send him far away so he can die over there.
**akin Tomás ákanara sináke.** When they told Tomás he was a leper, he became bitter.
The wind tore the house apart.

s: Rásenenra senénbobires iki jawen chósko paróbo.
e: A square always has its four sides equal.
They say that in ancient times the Brazilian punched an image made of pitch.
Upon hitting a log, the raft fell apart.
Roberto's house is already falling apart because it's very old.

s: Kósira chopán rásoikitai jawen yóra mechá iketian.
e: José is drying himself with a towel because he is wet.

s: Nato jiwín rastón non topónke rabé chónka píchika táeya.
e: We measured the circumference of this tree and it was twenty-five feet.
The lupuna log is very thick.

s: Nato xónora moa rástonai réranon akanwe.
e: This lupuna (tree) is already getting thicker; let's cut it down together.

s: Ráta meranra non ícha jawéki bénxoai.
e: We keep many things in cans.
Bring me ten empty cans.
The grandmother died of fright.
You scared me.
You woke up your little brother while he was sleeping.
Don't be scared, son.
Sell me two plates.
My body feels uncomfortable because I haven't bathed.
An ant was walking on my belly.
My enemy hit me when I was drunk.
I have Sína as an enemy.

s: Abion rabéra bóchikiax ráwinananke íjirisisio aki.
e: Two airplanes passed each other performing maneuvers in the air.

s: Motóronin kakínra nontín bóaibo non rawínke.
e: Going by motor (motorboat), we caught up to and passed those going by canoe.
That man has become my enemy.

s: Wáme raxka riki áni; bóe maín, payári, ámakiri, keshó jábo riki raxkáya.
e: The scales of the paiche (a giant Amazon fish) are large; the boquichico, the acarahuasú, the arahuana, the gamitana, and the bujurqui also have scales.
They say that the banknotes of the yacurunas (water spirits) are the large scales of the paiche.

s: Icha jónibora rároai, jaton awínbo rayá íketian.
e: Many men are happy because their wives are hardworking.
My son has become industrious even though he used to be lazy.
The llavarachi doesn't bark, it croaks in the water.
My father-in-law is kind.

s: Nokon wetsán rayósainbora jakóma shinánya iki.
e: My brother's mother-in-law is very mean.
to bump someone on the nose
to break one's nose
perforation through the nasal septum
nose hairs
long-snouted pig
short-beaked loro (parrot)
to cork
sharp at the tip
to sit in the bow
upriver
to reach the top

s: Náto riki réa; reánra jími óyoai.
e: This is the callocallo; the callocallo sucks blood.
Climbing the tree, I reached the top.
The man who was on the verge of death expired.
My father paddles the canoe from the bow.
Go to the bow of the boat.
bow of a launch or motorboat
tip of a machete
I smashed the bow of the canoe.
arrow tip

I have come from upriver.
Let's the two of us go a little upriver for a walk.
The **shetebo** have aquiline noses.
My son has gone ahead because he's running.

s: Non rekén pápara iká iki Arán.
e: Our first father was Adam.
older brother
They say our ancestors used to wear only cushmas (traditional robes) and not trousers.

s: Rekénhakinra en rabé witá bóke; jápekao westíorabicho.
e: First I carried two shungo baskets; afterward only one.
Many years ago a steamship came from Iquitos for the first time.
My uncle wants the pointed stick.
I'll go ahead first so I arrive quickly.

s: Nato bákera nokon rékena pekao iki.
e: This child is my second child.
We breathe through our nose.
They say other demons have long noses.
The tip of your nose is very big.
My nostrils are very narrow.
The woman ground the corn to make chicha (fermented corn drink).

s: Nokon poínra átapa pímati xéki réneai.
e: My sister is grinding corn to feed the chickens.
Go throw out the ground apacharama.

s: Bakénra jabé báke jíwi rekín meran réniai.
e: The child is putting a small stick into the other child's nose.
I am corking the bottle.
Mom is smoothing the large jar with a small stone.
After hitting a log, the launch capsized.

s: Károra íchayora jawéki boi réokooke Aweitia poíntiain.
e: A truck carrying too heavy a load overturned on the Aguaytía bridge.
The wake capsized the canoe.
Mom emptied the aguaje fruits from the basket onto the ground.
Your nasal perforation is very wide.

s: Monsónra jawen bóti nokon repíntiain repínke.
e: A Spanish speaker docked his boat at my port.
Let's the two of us go cultivate (the land near) the port.
The raft is docking; we're going to sleep here.
Here is the stopper; go plug the mouth of the bottle.
I cut myself with Dad's machete.

s: Nokon papánra wái akin jíwi rérake.
e: While clearing the garden, my father chopped down the trees.

s: Nokon titánra kóchi rérake átsa píaitian.
e: My mother machete-struck the pig because it was eating the manioc.
Send just your son on the motor (outboard-motor boat).
Even though we left the dog on the other side of the river, it just keeps coming.

s: Nokon papán náiron risbíra bakén ménoa resénbinake.
e: My father's rope shrank at one end when a child burned it.
While crying, the boy got himself all smeared with mucus.
My son has a runny nose when he has the flu.

s: Kósira janbíx rétekaake jawen awin jóni betan méraax.
e: José killed himself upon finding his wife with another man.
A man committed suicide by shooting himself.
Thieves are killers.
My brother-in-law killed a jaguar.
Look! Those two hens are fighting each other.
A drunk woman drowned.

s: Bákera kíni meran káketian jóiman réteke.
e: A child fell into a pit and suffocated.
My son filled the bottle with dirt.
My nose is stuffed up with mucus and I can't breathe.
They say that in ancient times the motelo (tortoise) had a very beautiful *réwe* flute.
I will paddle from the bow, and you will steer.
Cate's nose ornament is very shiny.

s: Papánra nokon mekén réyake ea xeyókin.
e: Dad produced a sharp pain in my hand when I rubbed it.
through here
upriver
The children want five-real coins.
The thief stole the money again.
What more do you want?
Even though I took the cow, it has come back.
They left again.
Look again, you.

s: Páparibira Rimán kái nóbetan píchika óxe ikí.
e: Dad is also going to go with us to Lima for five months.
Antonio ran away because he didn't want to pay his debt.

s: Píchika pácha waranka sórora en Víktor Tejada ribínke.
e: I owe don Víktor Tejada five hundred thousand soles.

s: En ribínketianra nokon pátoronin ea kénamake.
e: My boss had me called because I have a debt with him.
"÷"**-ya.** Division is done with the sign "÷".

s: Jatíribi ribírobora, páyo ikenbi, non pótaama iki.
e: Some books, even though they are old, we don't throw away.
The children are to draw.

s: Bákebo ja ribójo óinaki yóyo iti iki.
e: The students will discuss the drawing they saw.
Mom, I want to drink milk
We fish with the cast net.
The men net-fish at night so their catch won't be taken from them.
Pedro, give me your motorbike as a gift
The missionary gave me a new watch

s: Ríkatonin arós beára en márokin bíke.
e: When the peddler brought rice, I bought it from him

s: Nato ríkisiomanra non bákebo bená jói onámati iki.
e: In this lesson we are to teach the students new words.

s: Náto riki papán ríma; papán rimán kénshowe.
e: This is Dad's file; smooth it with it
Lima is a big city

s: Antónyo Ramíreznin wakán noa paránta píanaanketianra non rimántanke.
e: When don Antonio Ramírez's cow ate our bananas, we sued him

s: Jawen pátoroninra Tomás rimántanke jawen ribín kopíayamatian.
e: Tomás was sued by his boss because he wasn't paying his debt

s: Kápitan Kuriel inóntianra rimínyo sontárobo ícha Pachítian beá iki.
e: In the time of Captain Curiel, many soldiers of the Lima government came up the Pachitea River
The lemon is sour

s: Bátarimonakinra non jáneai jawen jáne iketian.
e: We call it sweet lime because that is its name
This is Mom's lemongrass; she planted it

s: Motóro yámaketian apáokanike rímotiro akin ján tapán bóti.
e: When there were no motors in the old days, they made rímotiro oars to steer rafts and boats
What community is this man from?
Where is your father?
Many years ago, when soldiers fought, they stabbed each other with lances
On the Ucayali there is no marona bamboo, only paca (a bamboo species).
linen cloths

s: Rínosirontira jáke Ajírikain jaínoax Asiain. Ja yóina riki xoá, itan kikínbires iwé. Játiribibo riki rekíain rabé o westíora machánya.
e: The rhinoceros lives in Africa and in Asia. This animal is fat and very heavy. Some have one horn on the snout, and others have two

s: Rínsira jáke Tibítoain, Nóriti Amirikain, jainoax Orópain. Ja riki misho jisá. Jawen jína máxkoshoko. Jawen ráni riki keshtó. Jawen bíchi riki kopíora.
e: The lynx lives in Tibet, North America, and Europe. It resembles a cat, but its tail is shorter. Its fur is valuable in the market.

s: Ríonra jáke Ajírikain jainoax Inirain. Ja rión bénera kímisha báritianyaniax ráni jókonai jawen texónko. Ja awínra íamai texónko ráni jókoni.
e: The lion lives in Africa and in India. At three years of age the male lion grows a mane on its neck, while the lioness does not.

s: Ríoparora jáke Ajírikain jainoax Asiain. Ja riki ániorama. Jawen jína riki nenké. Jawen yora iki wisón toró torótani.
e: The leopard lives in Africa and Asia. It is not very big; its tail is very long; its body is spotted with black.

s: Ríosenra jatíbi néte oínke; jatíbi jónibo nato netén ikáboribi.
e: God watches over the whole world and the people who are in it.
They say that shamans, upon drinking ayahuasca, see God.
many gods
to worship idols

s: Ríosen néte ikáinra jawen kátotabo bonónxikanai.
e: God's chosen ones will surely go to paradise.
It's going to rain now because the thunder is sounding.
The musmuque bit me when I grabbed it.

s: Nokon rirós masáketian masá shínanira ea íitai.
e: I am sad because my watch has broken.
The priests pray.

s: Ea chónka mítoro risbí máromawe chaí.
e: Brother-in-law, sell me ten meters of rope.
He twisted the wire.
The woman is giving herself a beating.
Because Raúl did not come to school on time, he got a beating.
My mother whipped my son.
I beat the dog when it eats up all the fish.

s: Rósara janbíx rishkíke yoshín ja meran jíkiketian.
e: Rosa whipped herself because a demon had entered her.
Bring the whip so we can whip Miguel.
One meter has ten decimeters.
a group of ten and a half
Subtraction is done with the sign "-".
Don't you want to buy scraps of cloth?

s: Enra rítira a onánke —Ikira Antónyo ítai.
e: Antonio says, —I already know the letter a.
The liter is a measure used to measure liquids.
My grandmother has whitish spots on her feet.
—I've found a bad omen. —Where? —Here it is.

s: Moátian ápaokanike waxménya kéntikan roánkabi mápokin, tári, chitónti anón ixbon; néte xabáketian oínkana moákaya aká chitónti betan tári jakón kenéya.
e: Long ago they would catch the toad and cover it with a large pot, putting cotton inside so the toad would make a cushma (robe) and a pampanilla (loincloth). The next day, when they uncovered it, they would see that the pampanilla and cushma had already been made, both painted with beautiful designs.

s: Nokon táera róake, ompáx kobiman ménotax.
e: My foot has turned whitish because I burned it with boiling water.
They say that when the huancahui bird sings, people die.
—A dog made a sound of bad omen. —How did it sound? —As if it spoke.
In the old days, when there were no iron axes, they felled trees with stone axes.

s: Rókarokara jáwetianbi jawen awín betan pótaananyosma, iki, jatíbitianriki jabé.
e: The tokón and its mate never separate; they are always together.

s: Ishtoxónra en pótake rokón ea rétenoxon yátana.
e: The crazy man grabbed me to kill me, but I escaped running.
My brother went crazy.

s: Rókotoronra ákai ísinaibo pótekin xenabo tsekanoxon.
e: The doctor operates on some sick people to remove intestinal parasites.

s: Báke pikóyamaitianra rókotorbaon ákai aínbo xátekin.
e: When a baby cannot be born, the doctors operate on the mother.
The spirits of the lupuna (kapok tree) turn into healers.

s: Nokon xéta péketaton ea chéxayoraitianra, en rókotoro bóyamake.
e: I sent for the dentist to fill my decayed tooth that was hurting me a lot.

s: Moátianra Róma jonibaon nómiro akín akátiai: 1 akín rítira I, jaínxon 5 akín rítira V.
e: In ancient times, Roman numerals worked like this: 1 corresponded to the letter I, and 5 corresponded to the letter V.

s: Nokon pápayosi riki romén chéata yobé ikáxmabi.
e: My grandfather is addicted to tobacco, even though he is not a shaman.

s: Nokon bakénra róme jótiai, jawen wétsa betan jonéxon.
e: My son is smoking, hidden together with his brother.
Don't smoke a cigar; you are not a shaman.
This is my father's cigarette.

s: Jaton báke ísinatianra yobébo rómexeixon xoón ama kanai; já chíte akanai téomakin.
e: When their children get sick, the parents make a cigarette so shamans can blow the smoke on the children and then hang the cigarette butts around their necks.
When the ground gave way, the ojé tree fell into the ravine.

s: Ronín riki áni, nenké, rastón, jáinoax kenéya.
e: The yacumama is large, long, thick, and patterned.
**jaín jáabiribi.** the yacumama lives in the water; that's where it dwells.
The terrestrial yacumama is black in color and is not venomous.
On Monday we will continue the work.
The little bowl Mom made is very pretty.

s: Miaronki yómetso iki irákanai jatíbi aínbobo.
e: All the women say that you're a thief.

s: Papánronki píchika sapén jáinoax chósko wáme réteke.
e: They say papá has killed five manatees and four paiche.

s: Min jawéki Tomásen xobón pótayamawe; yómetsoronkiai.
e: Don't leave your things at Tomás's house; they say he steals.
–Might your husband have seen my son? –They say he has.

s: Játianki jóni káa iki, jákiribi jawen xobón.
e: Then, according to the story, the man returned to his house.
Careful! The snake can bite you.
There is no antidote for the bite of the loro machaco.
The guacamayo machaco is yellow and venomous.
The yacu jergón is speckled with thin black stripes, and it is venomous.

s: Róno riki jonín jáne, rónoribiriki yóina.
e: *Róno* is a man's name and also the name of an animal.

s: Nonra ákai rónokáxo akin níshi xókaxon, nónti rénexeeti akin.
e: We strip vines from the forest and make a braid to tie down the bow of the canoe.
The woman braids her hair.

s: Ronón ewara jéne meran jáke; aínbo jímiaxbí jenénko náshiketian yótoai.
e: The boa lives in the water and bewitches a woman when she bathes in the water despite her menstrual flow.
My son is hanging up above.

s: Nokon titánra paránta rontánke; nokon poínra jawen yámikenti róntanai.
e: My mother hung up the bunch of plantains, and my sister is hanging up her aluminum pot.
The red howler monkey is reddish in color and is found in troops.

s: Róomaban riki áni jíwi; jawen bími riki móxaya. Isábaonra jawen bími píai; jenénko páketaitianra yápabaon píai.
e: The *róomaban* tree is enormous in size, and its fruit has spines. Small birds eat the fruit, and when it falls into the water, the fish eat it.

s: Máioshiainoax ábion nóyaara jawen róon moá níshnoke.
e: The plane that was flying from Pucallpa disappeared little by little along with its noise.

s: Nokon bákera róookon ike; jatíribi bákebora íamake.
e: My son had whooping cough, but the other children didn't.
Mother's clay jar shattered into pieces when it fell.

s: Nokon pátoronin ispíkora rórokooke, bóchikiax páketi.
e: My boss's mirror shattered into pieces when it fell from above.

s: Titán kémpo ákaira bakén jamákin róro-
e: **ke.** The mocahua that mother was making was crumbled to pieces underfoot by the child.

s: Enra máitonko róroke; nokon papánra mátsi róroai.
e: I have crumbled a ball of earth, and my father is crumbling a piece of ice.

s: Ja xóntakora jatíbi jónibaon moa rótoke, jakóma íketian.
e: That young woman has been rejected by all the men because she is bad.

s: Nato konxán xatera moa rotó iki; páyo íketian rótokana.
e: This cedar log has been rejected because it is rotten.
By being too slow to go, I was left rejected.

s: Wétsa jéma jakón íti shínani káxa ea rotóke.
e: I went to another town thinking the situation would be good, but I became disillusioned.

s: Nokon pápara rotóke, Kósiiba téeti káxbira joríbake.
e: My father became disillusioned when he went to work with José, but since he didn't like it, he came back again.
The child spilled the beads.
The ungurahui fruits spilled onto the ground from the basket.
The people who were gathered were chattering and making a lot of noise.

s: Sabán pei mótsaxon mápoki non ákai mapón chéxaitian; játian bénxoai.
e: For headache, we apply the crushed leaf of the *sabán* shrub mixed with water, and then one gets well.
They say that if a person is buried in a blanket, they turn into a jaguar.
We called out to him shouting, but he didn't answer us.
They say a demon shouts from inside the cave.
I am trembling with fear.
My grandfather is shivering from the cold.

s: Jawen samá xáteaxa nato jóni ísinai.

They say that where there are whirlpools, there are villages of water demons.
The *ronsapa* stings like a wasp.
They say that if a *ronsapa* lands on someone, that person will suffer from some illness.
Look at this cute little child.
Extend your hand.
I extended my hand as a signal.
Papá raised the stick as a signal.
The heron ate the tiny fish.
The nurse gave him an injection because the fever wouldn't go down.
As Saint John's day approaches, the season of wind and cold weather sets in.

s: Nato jonín kotón kewera sankén iki.
e: This man's shirt embroidery has a firm, attractive appearance.
The embroidered shirts for sale have embroidery with a firm, attractive appearance.
They say the dragonfly is the demons' airplane.

s: Non santíra kókoara noa jisóntan jisóntaai.
e: When we eat watermelon, we urinate a lot.
My little daughter wants her *santo* toy.

s: Katénra jawen báke sánto bixónhibake Máioshiainoa.
e: Yesterday Cate bought her daughter a doll in Pucallpa.
They say the Holy Father calmed our ancestors.

e: When we wear shoes for the first time, our feet sweat.

**yónatai.** This child has a fever because he has measles.

s: Min noa sároránxonwe, jáinoa nobé ráenanaibo.
e: Greet our friends who are there for us.

e: Your good friends here send you their greetings.
Fleshy plantains are expensive now.

s: Nokon bákera en chópa bená sáwemake.
e: I dressed my son in new clothes.

e: My son doesn't want to put on his shoes, but I put them on him while he sleeps.
Papá is dressing himself in his new cushma.
I put on my shoes.
The thieves stole my mother's garments.

The mouth of a hole that is deep underwater appears when the water level drops.
They say that long ago women wore a floor-length skirt.
From Auquía on upstream, there are abundant *manta blanca* catfish.

I killed the taricaya turtle while it was bubbling as it came out.
There are isula ants outside.

My brand-new knife has already broken.

e: Now they are cutting the lupuna trees down to exactly five meters.
A square has equal sides.
Now the end of the month is approaching.

s: Náto bái sénenainko riki nokon xóbo.
e: At the end of this road is my house.

e: Nowadays there are many people throughout the world.
My children weigh the same.

e: Even though we worked equally, they paid me less than the others.
I finished cultivating my garden.

e: This food is not going to be enough for everyone.

My son likes to drink chapo made from pleasantly ripe plantain.

The soldiers march well.
Tell it to us with perfect clarity so that we understand it.

s: Nokon shinánbiribira wétsabaon shínana keskama iki.

s: Móara nato bákeranon ríbiritaya iki, shinán ákai ikáx.

e: This stupid woman is of no use to her husband in anything.

s: Nato bákeranonra shinánhoma iki; jákopira shinánbenoke.
e: This young man is forgetful; that's why he forgot his things.

s: Jatíbi rasénenbires tonrón iki. Shinánkayata, piróta jáskara tonrón.
e: Anything perfectly round is a sphere. For example, a ball is a sphere.
The clothes mom washed have already dried in the sun.

e: They say that in the old days grandmothers used to cry whenever there was thunder, thinking of their loved ones who had already died.

s: Yóashiko Inkán shinánketianronki rabé jóni kapénike.

s: Nato báritian xonón téetira en shínanai.
e: I have decided to work at the lupuna (giant ceiba tree) this year.

s: Nokon pápashoko mawáketianra en westíora simánan masá shínana iki.

s: Koríki yómetsoakanara en meskóbo shínana iki; ján jawékiati yámaketian.

s: Nokon pápashokonra shinítapon ati onán ikátiai.
e: My grandfather was very skilled at making cashimbo pipes.

s: Nokon papánra róme jótiai shinítapoman napóxon.

The pichico tamarin is very easily frightened.

Dad teased his brother-in-law.
The man courted the woman with little jokes.

e: If we're given a nickname since childhood, we won't be able to erase it when we grow up.
Dad told a joke.
Coatis eat centipedes.
I crossed the river.
The dog crossed over from the other bank.

e: This woman suddenly spilled water from her clay jar, because she was embarrassed in front of those around her.
Mom's chicha is spilling because the clay pot has cracked.

s: Nato kárapintirora konxán ati shínani janbíx shókikaake mekénki.
e: This carpenter, trying to drill a board, drilled through his own hand.
Grandfather drills the teeth of the spider monkey to make a bracelet with them.
The carpenter drills into the heartwood because it is hard.
This little child wants to suck on a pacifier.
They say the spirits of the renaco (a strangler fig) are little dwarfs.
This cowardly young man doesn't want to go into the army.
The one who is dear to us is coming.

e: I'm also going to Lima next month.

s: Nato báke ménotara jawen bémanan shomón iki.

s: Shontá —ikira noa íkai nokon báke aínbo akí.
e: We say, "Little girl!" when addressing our daughter.

e: "Fix me some food, little girl; I'll pay you."

When the guard whistled at me, I got scared.

e: When the teacher calls us with the whistle, we go into the school.
My friend stole a guard's whistle.

s: Oi bexónra, moa shórokin noa mecháake.

The *showáwa* bird sings at night.

barley for making bread
barley bread

A zebu gored a man with its horn and almost killed him.
The child cries because he doesn't want to eat onions.

s: Non sibóriaya jóno piáronki ochíti mecha nótsiai.

The child blows a whistle.

s: Asókaro sakora xoyán pékake; ja pekénra asókaro síike.
e: The rat made a hole in the sugar sack, and as it spilled the sugar made a trickling sound.

cement house

s: Bákera en sináake nokon koríkinin yómetsoa kopí.

s: Maístoronra ískoiranko sínta mítoro beti iki.

s: Bákera sintóranin yómetsoke jawen papán jishnóma.
e: The child stole the belt without his father noticing.

s: Chirápa riki kánchis siónya: joshín, oxna panshin, panshin, yankón, yankón paxná, amíkeska, joshín oxná.
e: The rainbow has seven colors: red, orange, yellow, blue, light green, violet, and pink.

s: Nokon titánra nanén jawen chitónti siyón ake.

s: Jónira yamé sión ikai pórokan chéxaa, jato oxá rátei.

My father served his boss.

s: Enra jíwi néaa ikáinoa westíora xáwi siwínke.

s: Koáratianínra jawen ispára siwínke, jóni rakéakin.

s: Xomóxkini meranoara nato bakén yomán siwínke.

s: Nokon ponyánra moa soá iki niskanoma.

s: Nokon jáne moa soá ikénra, en moa Kakónko káyamai.
e: My name has already been erased, so now I won't go to Caco.

s: Nato aínbora kikínbires soí iki; jákopira jaón kéenkanai.
e: This woman is very charming, and that's why men love her a lot.
My mom's hair is very glossy.

s: Chónka jónira téeti káke káchio; sókotara ísini banéke.
e: Ten men went to work in the forest, and six ended up sick.
My community is six river bends away.

s: Bonán tékaara nokon bakén rekín somónke.
e: My child's nose swelled up because a isula (bullet ant) bit him.

s: Binán tékaara nokon mekén somón iki.
e: My hand is swollen because a wasp stung me.

s: Nato jonín táera somónyora iki tatoxbatax.

e: This woman's hair is puffed out because she doesn't comb it.

the one who waters the seedlings
