s: Wapínkenaman ikára epán íso tonbo méraxon rabé réteke.
e: My paternal uncle found a troop of maquisapas (spider monkeys) in the renaco and killed two.

s: Oínyosma ikáxa wapóro óinax nato báke ráketai.
e: This child had never seen a steamboat and was afraid when he saw it.
Yesterday he went to Iquitos by launch.
A motor vessel sank at the port of Pucallpa.
There is no train in Iquitos.
When the airplane comes, please do not flee.
They say that a commander fell from the bridge of the steamboat into the water.
My canoe went in under the stern of the launch.
The house frame made from the wood of the *wárakeni* tree lasts a long time.
The child burned himself on the hot boiled squash.
We make chicha (a fermented drink) from squash.

s: Nokon papánra píchika pácha waránka sóro ribínke.
e: My father owes fifty thousand soles.
naxa aínbobo báchinananke.** The women fought pulling each other's hair when they got drunk on guarapo.
A man, full of rage, drank barbasco and died.

s: Papánra warókanin axón átsa xáki pótsiai.
e: Papa squeezes the grated manioc by putting it in the tipití.

s: Amaabira je, min ámaabira, je, warón rakáyamai, je. Eara rakáyamai, je.
e: Although I take to drinking, although I drink for you, drunk I do not lie down. I do not lie down.
The boss gave papa a lantern.

s: Westíora wása tonbo oínxonbira en réteyamake tóoatioma íxon.
e: I found a troop of frailecito monkeys, but I did not kill them because I had no shotgun.

s: Ino jóaitianronki jóni máshi meran míimeenike; játian moa káa pekao máshi wásameeta iki.
e: Long ago, a man buried himself in the sand of the beach when he saw a jaguar; when the jaguar had gone, the man brushed the sand off his body.

s: Titánra jawen chitóntinin ika máipoto wásake.
e: Mama brushed the dust off her pampanilla (loincloth).
Sweep the emponado (palm-slat floor) with this broom.

s: Nato bakénra en kaímito tsamana ea wásanaanke.
e: This child scattered the caimitos I had piled up.

s: Wasányakati xéaaxa nato jóni mécha iki.
e: This man is a good fisherman because he drank the sap of the *wasányakati* vine.

s: Ráma min awín washínoxiwe —akinki shinón ánike.
e: It is said that long ago the monkey said to a man: —Now you are going to deny your wife before the others.

s: Jawen átapa washíketianra yobé jonín aínbo réteke.
e: A sorcerer killed a bewitched-ed woman because she had refused him her hen.

s: Bakénra jahuen papán machíto wásinapon pótake.
e: The child threw his father's machete into the middle of the tall *wási* grass.

s: Non wásikoma chiáxka óinaronki jawéki akín kéxmiati iki.
e: They say that when we see a *wásikaman chiáxka* bird, our garden plot or something similar may turn out uneven.

s: Wásimanamamea kámpabora siná ikátikanai ráeamabo ikásh.
e: The campa (Asháninka people) of the Gran Pajonal were fierce because they had not been civilized.

s: Nato xóbora moa wásnoman wéxea iki.
e: This house is already full of spiderwebs.
He drank piripiri hoping to cure himself, and he died.

s: Nokon kotón waxá íketianra ea ránsatiain káyamake.
e: I did not go to the dance because my shirt was torn.

s: Nónti waxara áni iki; rámara noa jéne bóchoai —iki iká iki.
e: He said: —The crack in the canoe is big, and now it's going to fill up with water on us.

s: Nokon chiárextira en wáxake, yómetsonin chíbana íshtokin.
e: I tore my pants when I ran fleeing from a thief.

s: Tóoaka bóchikiax pakékinronki jonín nónti rebo róokan wáxanike.
e: They say that once a shot howler monkey fell onto the bow of a man's canoe and split it.
I threw away the pampanilla because it had already torn.
The cedar that papa felled (with an axe) split when it fell.

s: Papán ícha mapó beára nónti waxáke.
e: The canoe split because my papa carried too much clay in it.
The son burned his mother's loom heddle.
My papa is making a cotton garden plot for my mama.
Sit here.

s: Non káya bichínxonronki yóshiman pótai weánko.
e: They say that when a demon takes our soul, he throws it into a shadow.
Reddish water came from the Tambo River.

s: Jénepanshinya wéamanra báritian kabóri ícha iki.
e: In the dry season taricaya turtles are abundant in the Jenepanshea creek.
This child bailed out the dirty water.
Right now they entered the worship service.

s: Xétaoma ikaxa nokon títashokon kebí wéita iki.
e: My grandmother's lips are sunken because she has no molars.

s: Icha táshi wéita ikaxbira nato mísi táshioma iki.
e: Although a lot of salt went into it, this humita (corn tamale) is not salty.

s: Kikínhakin xépoyamaara xéni botirian ompáx weíke.
e: Water got into the oil bottle because it wasn't well covered.

s: En jóa bánaara moa barín wekánhake en ompáx tachíamaa.
e: The flowers I planted wilted from the sun and because I didn't water the roots.

s: Chóyachakin witáxonki wekíosi iki; ikáxbi benkéx táe máxkoshoko.
e: They say the legs of the chullachaqui demon are very bowed, and that one foot is smaller than the other.

s: Ja rábo wekíra bakén jamáke, íshto kakín.
e: While running, the child stepped on that bent nail.

s: Min táe wekía íketianra mia wáiroron bóyamake.
e: The guard hasn't taken you away because your foot is bowed.

s: Yoshínxatanronki jawenwetía iki, ján jóni yatánti.
e: They say the clown demon has his hook for grabbing people.
From the heat of the fire, this nail bent in the middle.

s: Nato jónira wékoti níai, páenama ikaxbi.
e: This man walks staggering, without being drunk.

s: Moa kímisha óxe ríki nato jóni ísina; jákopira moa wekóke.
e: It's been three months since this man got sick, and now he has gotten worse.

s: Moátianra nato jóni sinámatani iká iki; rámara moa wekóyorake.
e: Before, this man was a bit hot-tempered, but now he is worse.
This disobedient child got caught on something.
The child hooked his ear with the fishhook.

s: Míshkiti námi weméya íketianra átapanin námi píamake.
e: The hen couldn't eat the meat because it was hooked on a fishhook.

s: Yamé nókotaxa noa wenénhain óxaa iki.
e: Arriving at night, we slept in a cleared spot.

s: Jaín chíi ketéati epán wenénhaketianra titán áke.
e: Mama lit the fire to cook after that my uncle had cleared the forest.

s: Kónxaman téetaibaon wenénhainra noa nókota iki.
e: We arrived at the place where the loggers had made camp.
I made him stand even though he could no longer walk.
When he fell, he stood up again instantly.
When the authority arrived, the people stood up.
After drinking liquor, the men get agitated and fight.
There was a commotion at the dance.

s: Wéntameexonra binán rabé jóni tékake; wétsara jabáketian áyamake.
e: The wasps swarmed and stung two men; the third escaped and nothing happened to him.
When the shotgun went off, the herons scattered.
The police stirred up the people when they were gathered at a party.

s: Yóashiko Inkanronki bína wentánkatitai jaíba mérati bókanaitian.
e: They say the Stingy Inca made the wasps swarm when people went walking near where he was.
Don't scatter the hens.
When I hung it here, the child kept looking for it.

s: Papán íso tóoakara jíwi póyaman weóke.
e: The spider monkey my papa shot hung itself from the branch.

s: Oa paránta texkan wéotara pitsón píai.
e: That hanging bunch of bananas is being eaten by the parakeet.

s: Nato jónira janbíx wérameeke, páenama ikáxbi.
e: This man fell on his own, but he wasn't drunk.
When he was drunk, papa pushed the large jar.
The shirt I bought is very threadbare.

s: Básiora ísinaxa jawen píshi wére iki.
e: From being sick for a long time, his ribs stick out.
The firewood will run out; spread out the logs of the fire.

s: Oi béti keska ikáxbira moa naíkoin wésnata iki.
e: Although it looked like it was going to rain, in the end the clouds cleared away.

s: Rámara wéstiakin yónatai; bakíxa íoraa íibake.
e: Today he has very little fever; yesterday he was worse.
The corn I planted grew sparse.

s: Kakín, non rétea iki westíora yawíx, rabé jóno.
e: On the trail, we killed one armadillo and two collared peccaries.
The cat took the smoked meat from the hanging basket.

s: Nátora ea kéenyamai; wétsakaya ea méniwe.
e: I don't want this one; give me another.
Some days I go to the market.

s: Atapa riki, wétsa áni, wétsa ánima.
e: Some hens are big and others are small.
My brother bought a new motor.
He was going by canoe with his sister and it capsized along with her, alongside her.

s: Jawen wetsán chópa yámaketian nóibaxonra, jawen kotónbi nato jonín ménike.
e: This man took pity on his cousin who had no clothes, and gave him his own shirt.

s: Moa jenén réteainbira jawen wetsán bíke.
e: When he was drowning, his cousin saved him.

s: Nokon titánra jawen wétsa kenéati onámaa iki.
e: My mama taught her cousin to make designs.

s: Jawen wétsabi onányamaxonra, náwares shinánke, sáyayaiketian.
e: He did not recognize his own cousin; he thought she was just a mestiza because of the dress she was wearing.

s: Nato báritianra ea moa jiwín téewetsayamai.
e: This year I am not going to work in timber again.

s: Wanín wexáya non bóo méskoxon ménoaronki bóshtiti iki.
e: They say that to make our hair curly we must burn pijuayo palm shavings mixed with our hair.

s: Nókona ícha wexá jáaxbira mókaoma iki.
e: I have many darts, but they are not poisoned.

s: Jawen wexáchitaran átira en waxmén béke.
e: I have brought cotton to make cones on the darts.
When I grabbed the cat, it scratched me.

s: Wéxati riki ján jóni mapónko xáteti sinákin.
e: The ushate is used to make cuts on a person's head.

s: Jáskara wexébira jaton ríka xobon bokánke chóroti átipanyamaxon.
e: They took the tangled net home because they could not untangle it.

s: Ja wexé chóroti onányamaxonra jato nóshikanke.
e: Because they could not untangle their net, they broke it.

s: Anirikan ákaibaonra jaton ríka wéxekanke ícha jóxobawin mápoxon.
e: The net fishermen tangled their net when they caught many white súngaro catfish.

s: Papán risbíra nato bakén wéxeke; rámara noa nótsinai.
e: This child tangled papa's rope; now he's going to be angry with us.

s: Titánra nato yomán pótake moa wéxeta íketian.
e: Mama threw away this thread because it was already tangled.
I scratched myself with my own fingernail.

s: Koshín weyónkinra titán jawen báke pákeke.
e: The mother made her little daughter fall by rocking her too hard in the hammock.
**téshke, siná ishon.** While my brother was swinging, a rabid dog bit him.
They say the boa is the hammock of the water spirits.
to apply (achiote/annatto) to the leg
This tapir fat gives off a strong smell.
The net fishermen left my canoe with a strong smell.

s: Nato kampán tárira wíake, ícha néte pátsatama ikax.
e: This campa's cushma (robe) has a strong smell because he hasn't washed it for many days.
When a gale came, we began to paddle hard.
This child is a big crybaby.
Thinking of their fellow countrymen, they wept.
That man is about to cry; don't speak to him.

s: Kímisha pácha waránka sóro yómetsoakanara ea winkáske.
e: I felt like crying when they robbed me of three hundred thousand soles.
A man killed his enemy with a pijuayo-palm war club.
They say the campa know how to dodge their enemies' bullets.
He passed by me, but I didn't see him.
The riverboat already passed by.

s: Rabé nétera noa jakónbires winókanke, nokon epán báke sontáro kátanax jóketian rároi.
e: We spent two very happy days celebrating my cousin's return from military service.
What happened to you?
A thing of the past should not be mentioned often.
We have come paddling upstream from there and are safe and sound.
He took the paddle his father-in-law had made for him.
A drunk man cut his own leg muscle with a machete.
Out of fear of this white man, the child hid.

s: Wírishokotonin béwakanara nokon kéen iki; náxbakan íkanara nokon kéema iki.
e: I like it when someone sings in falsetto, but not when they sing bass.

s: Rastón áti yóiabira witá tayánkin papán wiríshake.
e: Although he was told to make the posts thick, papa carved them and they came out too thin.

s: Nato jónira moa wiríshke xoá ikáti ibi.
e: This man has become thin after having been fat for a long time.

s: Moa íchayora béwaaxa jawen jói moa wiríshke.
e: His voice has become falsetto from singing so much.

s: Bákebora wíritain káti iki jawéki xóxoai oíni.
e: The students will go to the orchard to see the plants growing.

s: Moátianronki kóshi jónibo jakátiai, wiróx sékeaibo.
e: They say that long ago there were strong men who broke the *wiróx* tree with just their hands.

s: Ishto ea káinbira, wísaka ea banéke.
e: While I was running, I turned around when someone whistled at me.

s: Maístoronra ea kírika wisháya mároti yóike.
e: The teacher told me to buy a lined notebook.

s: Kírikara nokóke Rímameax; ja wishá oínxonra en onánke ján bémaa.
e: A letter has arrived from Lima; by looking at the writing, I can tell who sent it.

s: Nato kírika moa wishá íketian tsóabi mároyamai.
e: Nobody is going to buy this book since it's scribbled on.

s: Oi béaitianronki mái wíshati iki béyamanon ixon.
e: They say that when it rains, you can draw a line on the ground so it won't rain anymore.

s: Papán jakómaakin wíshaara nato wáme nami písike.
e: This paiche meat spoiled because papa slit it badly.

s: Enra wíshake jatíbi nato jóibo, tée ikénbi.
e: I have written all these sentences, although it has cost me much effort.
This child doesn't know how to write.

s: Wishía íketianra nato ochíti en onányamake, íno keska íketian.
e: I didn't realize it was a dog, because it had stripes like a jaguar's.

s: Yamébi motóro jóaitianra en mérayamake; jawen wishíbichoresa en oínke.
e: Since the launch came at night, I couldn't make it out; I only saw its wake.
This girl striped herself with huito dye.
This child cut himself with a knife.
Papa killed the howler monkey while it was eating wild guabas.

s: Póronapon wishnín íketianra en táxa tsákake.
e: Since there was fog in the middle of the river, I crashed my boat against a logjam.
This morning it was foggy for the first time.
**jawen bába wíshpoki rérake.** The grandfather cut his grandson's shin with a machete.

s: Non wishtín topónketianronki non báke pói ícha íkai.
e: They say that when we count the stars, our children will later have a lot of excrement.
We mix piripiri *noíwaste* with mahogany bark.

s: Nokon pápashokora wishtín méxoai óinax ratéke jáskara oínyosma ikáx.
e: My grandfather was amazed when he saw a satellite, because he had never seen one before.
A man is whistling from the other side of the river.
They say the Dark Inca was a black man.

s: Moátianronki kirínkoboki wísobo betan meskókashamakana iki.
e: They say that in the past the gringos did not want to mix with black people.

s: Chitóntira manón síkaxon wísoake, nato aínbaon.
e: This woman dyed her pampanilla black with the special *máno* mud.

s: Wísobimi máanai namanra sipán icha iki.
e: Where the little black *wísobimi* fruit falls, sardines are abundant.
It might rain; the sky has already grown overcast.

s: Min ea pinómpari nato witá tóewe —akinronki jonín íno aká iki.
e: They say a man told the jaguar: —Before you eat me, first split this shungo.

s: Jaskábi píkota ikaxa nato bakén witáx yósho iki.
e: This child has had a crooked leg since birth.
**ra paranta xóixon píai.** The Huitoto roast plantains and eat them.

s: Títara jawen tsábe betan wiwán károai kake.
e: Mama went with her sister-in-law to gather remocaspi firewood.
Yesterday I cleared the weeds from my garden plot.
I'm yawning because I want to sleep.
The cortadera grass grows very densely.
The anteater eats isula (bullet ants).
The motelo (tortoise) eats the fruit of the little *xaén mapán* tree.
The anona is sweet.

s: Wámera jókakin jawen xaká ratsáti iki.
e: To skin the paiche (a giant Amazon fish), the scales are removed first.
The crab likes to be in the palizada (a log jam).
The woman is grating cassava to make chicha.
plantain grater
Mats are made from the bud of the shebón palm.
Mom was cutipated by the *xampósha* plant.
to scratch the groin of
dark groin area
The house with the tin roof is hot.
The sun sets and takes all its heat with it.
The fruit of the tamamuri is edible.

s: Nokon áwininra yápa jéne xánaake. Kawé pinón.
e: My wife has heated the fish broth. Let's go eat.
During the dry season I feel hot.

s: Bári ishtón xánayamaketianra, non chópa mechábi sáweke.
e: We put on our damp clothes because there was no sun to dry them.
That child was born still wrapped in the placenta.
The black bee likes ripe bananas.
The lizard digs in the ground.
The little *xáne* bird whistles to announce a windstorm.
The mantona has designs on it.

s: Xanínra bákeai jíwi táno kíni meran.
e: The maracana gives birth to its young inside a dry, hollow tree.
The *xanínya* mocahua is used to store ornaments.
Fill in that little ditch with dirt.
The wild uvilla is tiny.
In that little cocha that dried up, there used to be carachamas (armored catfish).
The man choked on a fish bone.

s: Xápo jóa tóetara páro nápo mánai.
e: The kapok tree's pod has burst open and its seeds are falling into the river.

s: Mái xará ixónra jonín nónti bóke.
e: There was a landslide that swept away a man's canoe.

s: Jóxo kóchibo xaranra westíora wíso kóchi iki.
e: Among the white pigs there is one black one.
The sharara eats fish.
Let's go fishing with huaca.
Dad's cedro (cedar) log was swept away by the river current.
In the past, they used to cut trees with a stone axe.

s: Báke pikóketian ákanai jawen póko xátekin.
e: When a child is born, they cut its umbilical cord.
Shaving his beard, he cut himself.
In the past, they used to make a headdress from the macaw's tail.
The pejetorres has a big head.

s: Jóni wánononra xawén báke xói itai.
e: The *xawén báke xói* bird sings so that a man will get married.

s: Maxínkonia kikinxaman jainoa jawékiboriki arós jáinoax xáwi.
e: The main products of the coast are rice and sugarcane.
The carachama's shell is rough.
When I grabbed the carachama, it scratched me.
The grinding stone is used for grinding things.
for teeth to come apart

s: Oa jonínra íchayora atsa xéati xéai.
e: That man drinks a great deal of masato (a fermented drink).

s: Niwe xéaaxa, westíora báke ésteax mawáke.
e: A certain boy inhaled a poisonous vapor; his stomach swelled up and he died.
Welcome, stranger.
Houses are made with shebón palm leaves.
That child has gapped teeth.
It's good to brush our teeth with a toothbrush.
The boa coiled around the chicken.
The *xeké* iguana likes to eat taricaya (turtle) eggs.

s: Xéki riki chícha axon xéati jakón.
e: Corn chicha is a pleasant drink.

s: Xéki xéko riki botíria répoti ati.
e: Corn cobs are used to stopper bottles.

s: Tita betan pápara xóbo xémakayan yakáke.
e: Mom and dad are sitting outside at the entrance of the house.

s: Santós betán Yorántara arós chóshiketian xémeai.
e: Santos and Yolanda are shelling rice as they harvest it.
The ox is threshing the wheat.
The cassava worm is bright green.
Capirona firewood glows brightly when it burns.

s: Nokon jochínra jawen báke xenan bexonke.
e: My older brother brought guaba for his child.
When guaba rots, it dries up.
The man brought a gamitana (fish) that had a lot of fat.
That old mestizo man has scabies.
Dad's axe is very dull.
This is Mom's little stick made of cañabrava (wild cane).

s: Manánxaweronki noa nátexaxki, wanín jóaketiampariki xépishitai.
e: They say that when the motelo (tortoise) bites us, it doesn't let go until the pijuayo palm flowers.
José didn't want to drink and only wet the edge of his lips.

s: Xóbomeax píkokinra nokon wétsan jawen xóbo xepóke.
e: When he left his house, my brother closed the door.
The house door closed by itself.
Open the door.
The baby's incisor teeth came in.
Grandma no longer has teeth; she only has gums.
Woven bracelets are made from the maquisapa's (spider monkey's) teeth.
Grandma has no teeth; she only has gums.
Dad's tooth root swelled up.

s: Xetenronki yoashiko inkán chíi bíaki niwéabaya ói béaitinki pánanike.
e: They say the renahui protected the fire when the stingy Inca made it rain with a windstorm.
They say the Shetebo buried the Inca's son.
I smelled that dad's salted fish had gone bad.
The clay from Pucallpa is sticky.
The *xéto* fish also eats other fish.
Dad will roof his house tomorrow.
Mom is weaving a mat.
Two boys were racing. One completely passed the other.
Dad shot the gamitana (fish) with his *xexáya* arrow. The arrowshot gamitana carried off dad's two-pointed arrow.
There is a lot of bolaina in the purma (fallow field).
The motelo (tortoise) eats the fruit of the ubo.
I rubbed my own stomach when it hurt.

s: Nokon epánra bakísh ea tóbi xeyóibake.
e: Yesterday my uncle rubbed my dislocated bone.
thorax
Itching is relieved with lime juice.
The woman who arrived from the Lower Ucayali is very fat.
Dad scratched me yesterday.
Yesterday I scratched myself all day.
A skinny little woman quickly got fat.
When I cleared the weeds, I piled them all in one place.

s: Tíriko xóxoa xaranbora, téetaibaon xóbibo xóxoa
e: **mérake.** Among the wheat plants, the workers found weeds.
Grandpa's house is old.
—Where is the mouse? —It's on the roof.

s: Xóbomaxka akín senénbaaxa ea Máioxiain káai bokón tapan boí.
e: When I finish the ridge, I'll go down to Pucallpa taking a raft of cetico (a fast-growing riverside tree).
The mestizo has a lot of hair on his chest.
Fresh fish roasted right away is very tasty.
Mom roasted the fish on the grill.
Mother is peeling manioc.
They say the toucan sings to bring rain.
The man who got sunburned is peeling.
The woman's nipple got infected.

s: Xómi bepón rikí xéati noín pótanoxon.
e: The sap of the ojé tree is drunk to expel intestinal worms.

s: Rirós iki rabé xómoxa; óra ákai betan minóto ákai.
e: The clock has two hands: one is the hour hand and the other, the minute hand.
Throw me some fruit.
My brother has worked my garden plot for me.
The child is eating in front of the house.

s: Xonára kéyama iki; ikáxbi ícha tapónya iki. Nexbakanra jáke.
e: The renaco is a medium-sized plant, but with many branches that look like roots. It grows in swamps.

s: Nokon wetsán ea rishkibatara, ea xonanke.
e: I have a bruise because my brother hit me.
The locrero bird's egg is eaten.

s: Xóno ríki rastón keyá mébi áni bémaya.
e: The lupuna is thick, tall, with large branches and wide buttress roots.
The *xonón née* lizard lives in the weeds.
That young lady got married yesterday.

s: Cháira xonxín iwanke jawen awin kénai.
e: My brother-in-law just whistled to call his wife.

s: Xónxo riki mécha; jawéki bixonra béro tsékaxon píai.
e: The carnicero hawk is a skilled hunter; from the animals it catches, it plucks out the eyes and eats them.
The leaves of trees are green.

s: Paránta xóora paxa pítima iki, píti riki xoixon jóaxon.
e: Green (unripe) plantain isn't eaten raw; it's only eaten roasted or boiled.
Dad whistles to call mom.

s: Moátianra yoshanbaon xopán bánakatitai, rámara tson bánayamai.
e: In the past, old women used to plant secana, but now nobody plants it.
The man fell and hit his thorax.
**íketian.** The pigeon isn't eaten because we could easily get a dislocated joint.
The man pushes the raft with the motor.
The brother-in-law jabbed him in the sternum with a stick.

s: Miara ja xóxobo ja basón áti iti.
e: The plants must be planted in the container.

s: Non kókoti jawékibo riki xóxoai jawékibo.
e: Our fruit trees are members of the plant kingdom.

s: Xóxo báke riki jawen pápa onántima.
e: That child is illegitimate; it isn't known who his father is.
Corn germinates and grows fast and bears fruit.
The rat steals peanuts and eats them.
Tomorrow he will go to Pucallpa.
Tomorrow the child will bring aguaje fruits.
Come with the book.
During the festival the soldiers march with their leggings.

s: Wétsa netén westíora kánsa iká iki íaman nónononoi jawen bákeboya.
e: One day a goose was swimming in the oxbow lake with her young.
—Do you have a wife? —Yes, I do.

s: Nato aínbaon bákera róokoya iki; jáskara ikáxa, járibi jayá iki.
e: This woman's child has whooping cough; therefore, she must have it too.
The child has aguajes.

s: Titán chómora xéatioma iki; ja nokon wáatan chómoresa jayá iki.
e: Mom's jar doesn't contain any drink; only my aunt's does.

s: Nokon ochítira manánxawen yáaman piá iki
e: **pábikiain.** The tortoise's tick has stuck itself to my dog's ear

s: Enra nokon xóbo yabínke, yómetsobo jíkinaketian.
e: I locked my house so thieves would not get in.

s: Nokon títashokora yáe bénai kawánke níi meran.
e: My grandmother went to the forest to look for the fruit called wild cherimoya.
The woman is sitting.
The one sitting under the tree is looking at me.

s: Titán áni chomora jéma napon yakáke.
e: Mother's big jar is in the yard.

s: Páoyamanra westíora náwa yakáke non kaíbo xaran.
e: In Paococha a mestizo lives among our countrymen.

s: Westíora yakátira ráma kikínbires kopí iki.
e: Nowadays a chair is quite expensive.
Over there is our new community.
The earthquake shook the water.

s: Jéne meranoax yoshín píkotainronki, jéne yakíke.
e: They say that when a ghost came out of the water, it shook itself violently.

s: Yáma riki kaíakanai jawéki Piróain jaá.

e: They say that multitudes of bats can invade us when there is a long-duration eclipse.

s: Yamékirira ea íshtoai, nokon yóra jakón kopi.
e: I run in the mornings to keep my body healthy.

s: Eara káa iki níi meran yamékirishoko jawékiaamabi.
e: I went to the forest early in the morning without breakfast.

s: Eara yaméke Amakiria nawékinin. Jáskarabi joáxa ea Kakónko nokóke.
e: I spent the night in the bay of Amaquiría, and then arrived at Caco.

s: Enra yámi taxo ánoxon en texó káxke béke.
e: I brought a quinilla-wood post to make the axe handle.

s: Ikítoainoax joá wapóroninra yámi ícha máanhake.
e: The boat that came from Iquitos unloaded the iron.
How many meters wide is the metal mesh?
They say that the Yaminahua don't eat pumagarza (a heron species), because they fear being cutipados (spiritually harmed).

s: Yáminawabora nóki sinákanike, non jaton kaíbobo rétea shínanax.
e: The Yaminahua got angry with us because they thought we had killed their countrymen.
All blacksmiths have their anvil.
They say rust causes death.
Dad is making arrows to spear taricayas.
The smoked fish is piled up on the grill.

s: Yanchámara Aóiti páro kexa ícha iki.
e: Llanchama trees are abundant on the bank of the Aguaytía River.

s: Eara yánka jóke; tsóabira en mérayamake.

Nowadays we Peruvians are free.

You have come very late.

Today it grew late and turned cold.

s: Moa yantányora íketian, noa banékirana iki.
e: When it was already very late in the afternoon, we returned.
When it is cold, the fish get sluggish in the oxbow lake.

s: Chónka kiro ea asókaron mároketianra, jawen yápa mesó ea pátoronin ménike.

I am cutting ochomullaca for firewood.

s: Titánra chómo yasánke nontín ompax bíi kaxon.
e: The mother placed the jar in the canoe when she went to fetch water.

My brother was detained by the guards.
The dog is chasing the peccary.

s: Náto jónira kikínbires yóashi ikáx sínatai jáiba bokánketian.
e: Because he is so stingy, this man gets angry when there are visitors in his house.

s: Nokon pápashokora nokon wétsaki míshkitinin yóashike.
e: My grandfather stingily refused to give my brother the fishhook.
The fruit of the *yobán* tree is like a bean.
My grandfather is a sorcerer.
The sorcerer gargles a liquid with tobacco.

s: Bonsín riki ochíti keska, ikáxbi yobé.
e: The otter looks like a dog, but it is an enchanted animal.
The man is improperly asking that woman's father for her.

s: Nopatáx ikára yámikentin yobénke, mároti átipanyamáx.
e: Our neighbor improperly asked us for a pot; he could not afford to buy one.
books of sorcery and magic
Let's go eat some fruit.
I am planting chili peppers.

s: Nokon yóiabora en sénenhai; mínkayara senénayamai.
e: I keep my promises; but you don't.

s: Píti tsakaitúbira, nokon wétsa mécha jóniboki yóimeetai.
e: Every time a fish bites, my brother pretends to be an expert at mitayando (hunting)
This woman is a gossip.

s: Ino riki westíora yóina kikínbires siná, raké ikáxbi.
e: The jaguar is a very fierce animal, but also very timid.

s: Aínbaonra jawen béne wétsa aínboki yoínke.
e: The woman was jealous of her husband over another woman.
He spoke to me.
He said to me: —Don't go.

s: Maístoron mia yóiti iki jaskáaxon áti.
e: The teacher will explain to you how to do this.
If dad orders me, I'll bring the hen.

s: Tson yómetsoaketianki, nato jonín ea yóia.
e: When someone robbed him, this man accused me.

s: Yóiti bákera jawen titán moén áyamai.
e: The mother doesn't spank the child who is obedient.

s: Kónxaman téetaiboronki néte xabáti óchoma yáwakanike; westíora jónires íamanike yóiti ikáx.
e: They say that long ago some loggers turned into huanganas at dawn, and only one was saved because he was obedient.
The disobedient child fell into the fire.
The mother punishes the misbehaved child with a spanking.

s: Yóitima íxónra, bakén jawen papán xóbo ménoke.
e: Because he was bad, the boy burned down his father's house.

s: Náto chíiki páketa, bákera jákiribi yóitimake.
e: The boy who fell into the fire went back to being disobedient.
Those men rebelled against the Word of God.
The doctor's question is very difficult.

s: Nokon kokán yoká íketianra, náto átapa en bóai.
e: I am bringing this hen according to my uncle's request.

s: Jatíbi jawéki yokámis riki náto jóni.
e: He is a very inquisitive man; he asks about everything.
Because he is hungry, the man begs.
I asked for water
—Don't you know? —Ask Nima.
This child has gotten dirty with honey.
I bought thread for my wife.

s: Nokon títashokonra yomán ake jawen bába táriaxonti.
e: My grandmother made cotton thread to make a cushma (traditional tunic) for her grandson.

s: Yomén bépoman nóa méskitaronki tobí onánti iki.
e: They say that if we apply the resin of the *yomén* tree, we become masseurs and can heal fractures.

s: Jonínra yómerake bawín, moxóbaton, jainoax wetsa yapaboribi.
e: The man caught súngaro (a catfish), mullet, and other fish.
A thief stole a woman's bag from her.
A mestizo stole our watermelons.

s: Maxóchanto taxbá naman káketianronki yompán jenénko pakekin rátenike, játianbi káwetsatimakin.
e: They say that Maxóchanto went into the tahuampa (flooded forest); and that when a red chameleon fell into the water, it got scared and never came back.
He gave the child quite a few beatings.
He has healed completely.
Measles causes a high fever.
Since I have a fever, I feel cold.

s: Nokon wétsanra yoná ake, kirípi koshín ikín.
e: My brother had a fever from a bad flu.
smoked fish
The cat took the smoked food from the hanging plate.
Mom smoked the fish.
All blacksmiths have an anvil.
The palometa (a fish) feeds on the fruit that falls from the moena tree.

s: Nato asókaro sákora en yonó bóai.
e: I am carrying this sack of sugar because it's an order.
The new chief's mandate is carried out by the people.
The man fulfilled his job.
He ordered bananas to be brought.
**wáiroron yatánxon yónoke.** The guard caught the street kids and sent them to work.
Nowadays we Peruvians are independent.
Mom is making firewood from pashaca wood.

s: Nokon ochítira matsín aká yóotai chíi kexa.
e: My dog, when it's cold, warms itself near the fire.

s: Nokon wétsa yópa ixonra tóo akin xarára kéneke.
e: Since my brother has poor aim, he shot at the xarara (a snake) and it got away.
This man used to be a good hunter, but now he has lost his aim.

s: Nokon ochítininra ícha manánxawe bikátiai. Ikáxbira móa yópake.
e: My dog used to catch many tortoises. But now it has become used to track down many tortoises, but now it has become a poor hunter.

s: Non piá iki; ikáxbi non yóra yósmares iká iki.
e: We ate; nevertheless, our bodies were weak.
The trunk of the capirona (a tree) is slippery; that's why it's hard to climb.
Plants have roots and stems.
It is very good.
I came because he said something very true.
My head hurts a lot.
to struggle for food and clothing
having a need for food
I no longer need anything.

s: Enra jéne meranoa yóshiman boéxeti mérake.
e: I found a little *yóshiman boéxeti* fish in the water.

s: Jéne meranoáx yoshín pikotainronki, jéne yakíke.
e: They say that when a ghost came out of the water, it shook itself.
They say that the yacurunas come out onto the riverbanks at night.

s: Mawáyoshinra jóxo chópa sawéya iki, páeri keska.
e: The ghost wears white clothing like a monk's.
They say the forest demon dresses in black.
This child is not able to speak.
They say a woman gave birth to a baby with a deformed foot.
All crazy people are disobedient.

s: Yoshínkoshki non métotinin métoaronkin non métoti payóti iki.
e: They say that if we point at the rainbow with our fingers, we can get hurt.

s: Yoshíntetekanronki mékayao iká mapón ísobires píai.
e: They say the ghost hawk eats only spider monkeys, turning its head only to the right.
The man went crazy over a woman. The two of them drove each other crazy.

s: Sanánko xéaaxa jóni yoshínke, samá xáteax.
e: When the man drank sanango (a medicinal plant), having broken his diet, he became intoxicated.

s: Jónira jóboai pontónkoain, yóshini nawán jawéki méetax.
e: The man, having become contaminated by touching things belonging to other tribes, now has a tumor on his elbow.
They say the clown demon used to strangle people.

s: Yoshínxetaya keskara ián kexakea en mérake.
e: I found someone resembling the clown demon on the bank of the oxbow lake.

s: Nokon kanótira, yósho ikax, jakóma iki.
e: My crossbow has bent and it's no longer useful to me.
The Campa eat a lot of ashipa.
The old man came.

s: Papánra bákeranonbo jóketian jato bikín —jowé, yósi— ápakeke.
e: My dad received the young men and greeted them respectfully, saying: —Good day, sirs.

s: Ja jónira moa yósiora iki; jákopira míaareske.
e: That man is very mature; that's why he has beaten you.

s: Jawen kenínbira náto jóni móa yósiake.
e: This man's beard makes him look older.
My dad is already getting old.

s: Non piá iki; ikáxbi non yóra yósmares iká iki.
e: We have eaten; but nevertheless, our bodies remained weak.
My uncle got sick, and that's why he looks weak.

s: Yósma ikáxa, nato sontáro ráketai jawen rawíki.
e: This soldier is afraid of his enemy because he is a coward.
one who never comes

s: Náto jónira sináisma iki. Jáskara íketianra, játixonbi nóikanai.
e: That man is one of those who never gets angry. Because of that, everyone loves him.
That fearless one is following the fierce dog.
one who never knows

s: Sánjoan píshta ochómaitian yotán pakétara kikínbires mátsi iki, eára xéta sákisaki íkai.
e: When the feast of San Juan approaches, the season of intense wind and cold arrives, and I am shivering with cold.
My brother was walking only on the side of his foot; he must have sprained it.
Cloth made of jute lasts a long time.

s: Jawen yotó nítikoma íketianra, pápa jóyamake.
e: Dad didn't come because he was unable to walk, having been bewitched.
Two sorcerers bewitched my father.
The old woman who is coming is my mother-in-law.
Good morning, miss.
When the President arrived in Pucallpa, he spoke.
We conversed with the President.
This year the mango fruits went to waste.
The cook wasted the chicken soup.
